Executable Emoji
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-09
17:28:52 UTC
02:28:52 KST

Executable Emoji
This particular post comes out of left field a bit. I was playing around with a web application I had made - an online disassembler for the x86 - when I noticed that emoji were being encoded into the url.
I pasted a goat emoji, 🐐  and I noticed the encoding %F0%9F%90%90.
Now, if you're familiar with x86 assembly language at all, hexadecimal 90h is probably familiar to you. It's the opcode for a null operation or NOP.
I had a brief nerd chuckle over the thought that goats were the NOPs of emoji, but then I got curious. F0h on the 8088 is the LOCK prefix. This prefix is generally used to coordinate exclusive bus access with a coprocessor such as the 8087, but otherwise does nothing for most instructions on the 8088 and is ignored (this would change on later Intel CPUs). That leaves us with 9Fh. 
9Fh is LAHF. 
The entire goat emoji is valid 8088 machine code, a sequence that reads
lock lahf
nop
nop
As it turns out, the vast majority of emoji graphemes, as they are called, start with the sequence F09F. A dim little light bulb started to flicker above my head.  Could you actually write an 8088 program using nothing but displayable emoji?  
The idea is not without precedent. It has been well-established that executables can be generated with only printable ASCII characters - the most famous example probably being the EICAR test file, an ASCII string that is also a valid DOS executable that prints "EICAR-STANDARD-ANTIVIRUS-TEST-FILE!" and exits.
Other small ASCII programs were printed in magazines or distributed in other ways, such as the tiny terminal utility TCOM, the entire source of which is reproduced below:
XPHPD[0GG0G,0G51G31GB'(G+(G:u'0g?(G>(GE1G@arwIV_F*=US@>1|_,5wXNg-7muTu(4
1m0ss1k260s@3G1g360@3G0i7t2g3A1g350@3G2E1=0C1g350@3T2M0^\1g3>0@3T=1s2g0T
1g3;0@3ToN2g391g0t@3G0^F1k0s2?0@3T4
This is an interesting "emergency terminal" solution: if someone had no other means of loading an executable onto a computer system, it could simply be entered in via the keyboard.
It surprises me that the idea of directly executing emoji has apparently never been explored.
Hello (World)!
Of course, the first thing to do is attempt Hello World! in emoji. For space reasons and partly due to the pain of doing any sort of arithmetic in emoji, we will only print the string HELLO.
Here is the full program:
🐸☺️🐰🐎♐🗃️🧯🧯🧯🐮💗🦮♐🐰🐹🗃️🧯🧯🧯🧯💗🪗🧯😗🧮😗🧮😗🐮😪😔⭐
Pasted into a text editor and saved as UTF-8, no BOM, with a .COM file extension, the result should be 141 bytes with an MD5 sum of 0a5c91475ca2de33e36aacc2f0b7b840.
The disassembly of the entire program can be viewed here. If you have difficulty copying and pasting the emoji from blogspot, try copying them from that link.
Several emoji here may display as tofu, depending on your browser and what year you are reading this article.
 is the shovel emoji, introduced in Unicode 16.0 in 2024. These glyphs still take time to trickle down into font updates.
🪗 is the accordion emoji, added to Unicode 13.0 in 2020, but somehow still not visible in Chrome on Windows 10. Go figure.
 is the "Distorted Face" emoji and is brand new in Unicode 17.0, approved in 2025.
In theory, it should be possible to copy the relevant tofu character and preserve the representational bytes, but some operating systems and programs seem to struggle with the byte-preserving concept.
This program relies on a few undocumented 8088 aliases, and so requires a fairly accurate 8088 core to execute successfully. Let's see what it does in DOSBox-X with cpu cputype=8086:
Note the program starts with 🐸☺️. This sequence does some important setup and explains how we get a pointer to video memory. These emoji represent the byte sequence
F09F90B8E298BAEFB88F. 00000000  F0 9F     lahf
00000002  90        nop
00000003  B8 E2 98  mov ax,98E2h
00000006  BA EF B8  mov dx,B8EFh
00000009  8F        db 0x8FF09F9297, moves our video segment into DI. 0000012C  F0 9F  lahf
0000012E  92     xchg dx,ax
0000012F  97     xchg di,axF09F9783EFB88F, comes in clutch here:00000146  83 EF B8  sub di,FFB8hFFB8h is equivalent to addition by 48h. What's H's ASCII hex code? 48h.  Neat. 
Emojissembly Reference
Standalone Emoji
Open-Tail Emoji
Useful Gadgets
These are complete, useful sequences of multiple emoji.
BunnySad: 🐰😔 - Stack repair
This eight-byte sequence deliberately replaces the current stack pointer with FFF0h:
0000: F0 9F    lahf
0002: 90       nop
0003: B0 F0    mov al,F0h
0005: 9F       lahf
0006: 98       cbw
0007: 94       xchg sp,ax
The rabbit's final B0h consumes the sad face's leading F0h, loading AL=F0h. The second LAHF is followed by CBW, which turns that into AX=FFF0h; XCHG then installs it as the stack pointer.
This is how to recover after intentional POPs and keep asynchronous interrupt pushes near the top of the segment. It discards the current stack, so it is safe only when no return address or saved value is live. The old SP is left in AX.
BunnySnowParty 🐰☃️🐰😔 - Safe addition: DI += 48h
This 18-byte sequence advances DI by 48h (72 decimal), absorbs the snowman's dangling POP, and repairs the stack:
0000: F0 9F       lahf
0002: 90          nop
0003: B0 E2       mov al,E2h
0005: 98          cbw
0006: 83 EF B8    sub di,FFB8h
0009: 8F F0       pop ax
000B: 9F          lahf
000C: 90          nop
000D: B0 F0       mov al,F0h
000F: 9F          lahf
0010: 98          cbw
0011: 94          xchg sp,ax
The first rabbit consumes the snowman's E2h; B8h is a signed -72 immediate, so SUB DI,-72 adds 72. The snowman's final 8Fh consumes the next rabbit's F0h as the undocumented POP AX encoding 8F F0. The final rabbit/sad-face pair restores SP=FFF0h.
This was one of the first gadgets found. The eye and plate gadgets are usually more efficient, but this one is included for completeness.
PlateGoat: 🍽️🐐 - Increment SP and advance DI
The plate needs a following byte to complete its final 8Fh. A padding goat is a convenient harmless tail.
0000: F0 9F          lahf
0002: 8D BD EF B8    lea di,[di-4711h]
0006: 8F F0          pop ax
0008: 9F             lahf
0009: 90             nop
000A: 90             nop
B8EFh is the 16-bit representation of -4711h, so the LEA performs DI += B8EFh. The plate's 8Fh consumes the goat's leading F0h as undocumented POP AX; the remaining 9F 90 90 is LAHF; NOP; NOP.
Plates advance SP by two as well as moving DI a significant distance. Plates are excellent for pointer arithmetic, but their stack effects must be accounted for.
CatGoat: 😿🐐 - Absolute DI reset
The crying cat opens MOV DI,imm16. A padding goat supplies the immediate.
0000: F0 9F       lahf
0002: 98          cbw
0003: BF F0 9F    mov di,9FF0h
0006: 90          nop
0007: 90          nop
This eight-byte gadget resets DI to 9FF0h without depending on its previous value. If another emoji replaces the goat, its leading F0 9F still becomes the immediate, but its remaining bytes execute as a tail and may further change DI.
CamelWrite: 🗓️ + arithmetic + 📗🐪 - Generate and write a byte
The generic form is 15 fixed bytes plus the chosen arithmetic sequence. Here is the simplest concrete example, 🗓️🐮📗🐪, using a cow to add one:
0000: F0 9F       lahf
0002: 97          xchg di,ax
0003: 93          xchg bx,ax
0004: EF          out dx,ax      ; spurious OUT to B8EFh
0005: B8 8F F0    mov ax,F08Fh
0008: 9F          lahf
0009: 90          nop
000A: AE          scasb
000B: F0 9F       lahf
000D: 93          xchg bx,ax
000E: 97          xchg di,ax
000F: F0 9F       lahf
0011: 90          nop
0012: AA          stosb
On entry, DI is the real output pointer and AX contains the arithmetic seed. 🗓️ moves the seed into DI and saves the output pointer in BX.
The middle emoji sequence performs arithmetic on this temporary DI; the cow above adds one.
📗 restores the output pointer and transfers the computed low byte into AL, and 🐪 writes it.
The calendar also performs OUT DX,AX. The common startup establishes DX=B8EFh, a generally unmapped port. Use with caution on real hardware!
FrogStrap: 🐸☺️😖🐰😗😯😯😯😯😯😯😯 - Common register bootstrap
This 50-byte sequence obtains a known zero from the normal COM entry stack and establishes a specific register state:
0000: F0 9F       lahf
0002: 90          nop
0003: B8 E2 98    mov ax,98E2h
0006: BA EF B8    mov dx,B8EFh
0009: 8F F0       pop ax
000B: 9F          lahf
000C: 98          cbw
000D: 96          xchg si,ax
000E: F0 9F       lahf
0010: 90          nop
0011: B0 F0       mov al,F0h
0013: 9F          lahf
0014: 98          cbw
0015: 97          xchg di,ax
0016: F0 9F       lahf
0018: 98          cbw
0019: AF          scasw
001A: F0 9F       lahf
001C: 98          cbw
001D: AF          scasw
001E: F0 9F       lahf
0020: 98          cbw
0021: AF          scasw
0022: F0 9F       lahf
0024: 98          cbw
0025: AF          scasw
0026: F0 9F       lahf
0028: 98          cbw
0029: AF          scasw
002A: F0 9F       lahf
002C: 98          cbw
002D: AF          scasw
002E: F0 9F       lahf
0030: 98          cbw
0031: AF          scasw
🐸☺️ loads DX=B8EFh and leaves a dangling 8Fh. The first byte of 😖 completes POP AX, obtaining the known zero at SS:FFFEh and wrapping SP to 0000h; the rest of 😖 moves that zero into SI.
🐰 consumes the leading F0h from 😗 to make AL=F0h, after which CBW; XCHG DI,AX establishes DI=FFF0h. Seven SCASWs advance it to FFFEh.
The final state is DX=B8EFh, SI=0000h, DI=FFFEh, and SP=0000h.
The value of B8EFh in DX is within the lower portion of CGA video memory if used as a segment.
An additional 😯 can roll DI over to 0000h. The value FFFEh left in DI has conceivable uses as a -2 constant.
🐸☺️🐰🐎♐ - Load the CGA segment
This 21-byte sequence exploits the original 8088's undocumented segment-register alias to establish ES=B8EFh:
0000: F0 9F       lahf
0002: 90          nop
0003: B8 E2 98    mov ax,98E2h
0006: BA EF B8    mov dx,B8EFh
0009: 8F F0       pop ax
000B: 9F          lahf
000C: 90          nop
000D: B0 F0       mov al,F0h
000F: 9F          lahf
0010: 90          nop
0011: 8E E2       mov es,dx
0013: 99          cwd
0014: 90          nop
A Basic Loader
bits 16
org 0
    push di
    pop  si                         ; SI = encoded emoji data
    mov  di,0100h
    push di                         ; RET target after reconstruction
    mov  cx,RAW_SIZE
.decode:
    lodsw                           ; discard the fixed F0 9F prefix
    lodsw                           ; AL=third UTF-8 byte, AH=fourth
    aad  8Fh                        ; AL=(AL + 8Fh*AH) & FFh; AH=0
    stosb
    loop .decode
    ret                             ; execute reconstructed COM at 0100h
lodsw reads the two-byte prefix of each 'data grapheme', discarding it. The second lodswthen reads the 16-bit tail, which is converted to an 8-bit value with the magic constant 8Fh. The key here is a feature of 8088's aadinstruction that allows it to take a non-decimal base as an immediate.lahf is constantly clobbering AH, so this 17-byte decoder must itself first be constructed in memory. This can be accomplished with the CamelWrite gadget described previously.
A VGA Emoji Demo
Could you construct an emoji BIOS? An entire emoji operating system? Could we have EmojiDOOM?

Uber launches parking service following SpotHero acquisition, with an eye on robotaxis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-09
17:00:00 UTC
02:00:00 KST

Uber on Monday said it is launching a new service that lets customers reserve and pay for parking in major U.S. cities, about nine months after the ride-hailing company acquired parking app SpotHero.
The acquisition, announced back in February, gives Uber access to a network of 13,000 garages, lots, and valet services across more than 400 cities, the company said. And while Uber’s initial plans will focus on human drivers, the company also plans to leverage these parking spots to help the dozens of autonomous vehicle companies it has partnered with.
Uber said the parking spots could be used as staging and waiting locations for autonomous vehicles to help reduce congestion and deadheading, which refers to the miles a vehicle travels without a paying passenger or cargo on board.
For now, the company plans to focus on commuters driving their own vehicles. Uber said it will initially launch in 15 U.S. cities, including Atlanta, Austin, Boston, Chicago, Dallas, Denver, Los Angeles, Miami, Nashville, New York City, Philadelphia, San Diego, San Francisco, Seattle, and Washington, DC.
Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi indicated earlier this month that the company wants the app to be more relevant to commuters.
“Commute is one of our largest categories,” he said during Uber’s third-quarter earnings call. “And to be able to offer commuters an Uber to work, a pass to avoid surge, and parking if they want it when they want to drive is a great example of us building out our inventory of services to the commuter who is a top customer for us.”
The parking service is the latest in a series of efforts at Uber to build an ecosystem of products that keep customers engaged with its app for everything from hailing a ride and ordering food and groceries, to package delivery, renting cars, booking hotels, and connecting users with public transit and robotaxis.
Uber’s membership program, called Uber One, is a key part of that strategy. Uber One attracts subscribers by offering rewards and credits, perks that have helped the program grow to more than 55 million members as of September 30. For instance, Uber is offering members a chance to earn 10% back in credits on eligible parking reservations. Those credits can later be used for rides and Uber Eats orders.
Uber Parking can be accessed directly on the app’s homescreen. Users can enter their destination, select the date and time they need parking, and then review options on an interactive map. Users can filter the results to find self-parking, valet, garages, or surface lots. All pricing is shown upfront.
Once a user has found a parking spot, they can book after entering details about their vehicle, and use the payment method in their Uber wallet. Once they arrive at the parking spot, users will either scan a unique QR code or gain entry through license plate recognition. Uber said users will be able to cancel their bookings for free until the start time.

For the Best Buttered Noodles, I Always Add a Pinch of This
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-09
17:00:00 UTC
02:00:00 KST

Not Parmesan, Not Black Pepper: For the Best Buttered Noodles, I Always Add a Pinch of This
Every fall, my favorite go-to easy weeknight dinner is buttered fettuccine paired with a salad and protein. It’s an extremely satisfying meal that’s filling and always hits the spot. I always thought my butter-and-cheese pasta dish was great — until I tasted my brother’s buttered noodles. His pasta had a comforting, aromatic warmth that made every bite pack more of a punch than my own. When I pestered him for his secret, he revealed his trick: He swaps the standard plain butter for melted butter with a pinch of garam masala powder.
What Makes Garam Masala the Perfect Addition to Buttered Noodles
My brother’s hack was simple: Instead of using plain butter he added a pinch of garam masala bloomed in melted butter for a few seconds, then tossed in the hot noodles with Parmesan cheese.
Simple butter-and-cheese weeknight pasta can sometimes feel one-note and a little flat. Blooming garam masala (a mix of warm, sweet spices like cinnamon, clove, nutmeg, and cardamom) in butter coats the pasta with extra flavor, turning basic buttered noodles into a cozy, warming autumn dish. Yum!
How to Add Garam Masala to Buttered Noodles
- Melt two tablespoons of unsalted butter in a skillet over medium-low heat.
- Add a generous pinch (about 1/4 teaspoon) of garam masala directly into the warm melted butter and let it bloom for 10 seconds until fragrant.
- Immediately toss in eight ounces of freshly boiled, hot pasta noodles along with a splash of reserved pasta water.
- Remove the skillet from the heat and fold in 1/4 cup of freshly grated Parmesan cheese until silky and fully coated, then serve hot. Bon appétit!
Tips for Adding Garam Masala to Buttered Noodles
- Carefully watch the heat. Garam masala powder consists of finely ground spices that burn very quickly in hot butter. It’s important to keep the flame low and only bloom it for about 10 seconds before tossing in your hot pasta. This preserves its smooth, aromatic flavor.
- Always use fresh, high-quality Parmesan. Grating cheese fresh from a block ensures it melts smoothly into the warm, spice-infused butter. This helps create a silky sauce.
- Adjust the garam masala to your taste. Begin with 1/4 teaspoon of garam masala for a subtle, comforting flavor. If you’d like a bolder, more aromatic dish, increase the garam masala to 1/2 teaspoon.

Anthropic joins AI’s natural gas frenzy, buys $3.4B worth of turbines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-09
16:56:54 UTC
01:56:54 KST

AI’s power crunch has become so acute that Anthropic, a company that has generally avoided buying physical infrastructure, is spending $3.4 billion on natural gas turbines.
The AI company, which is planning to go public this year, is buying Caterpillar generators that equipment supplier OnePWR had originally ordered, according to a Financial Times report. The generators are capable of producing up to 1.7 gigawatts of electricity.
Historically, Anthropic has preferred to rent rather than buy. The company disclosed in its S-1 filing in May that it is paying SpaceX subsidiary xAI $1.25 billion per month through May 2029 to use xAI’s computing power.
“We expect to enter into additional similar services contracts,” Anthropic stated in the filing, meaning more deals to rent computing power.
But as demand for compute ramps up, the market for power has also grown increasingly uncertain, which may have forced its hand. The backlog for natural gas turbines stretches into the early 2030s, and queues to connect to the electrical grid can be just as long.
Anthropic’s purchase looks like a last resort.
According to the report, OnePWR ordered the turbines a couple years ago but couldn’t find financing to complete the purchase. Anthropic had planned to buy them from OnePWR but instead went directly to Caterpillar, the manufacturer.
It’s not clear why OnePWR was unable to secure financing despite Anthropic’s apparent interest as a customer. Whatever the case, Anthropic likely wanted to keep the generating capacity to itself rather than give a competitor an opportunity to snap it up.
AI companies have been ramping up their purchases of natural gas equipment and supplies in recent years. Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and Meta have all announced plans to build massive natural gas power plants to power their data centers on-site, rather than drawing from the public grid.
The binge has given a second wind to fracking, the drilling method used to extract natural gas from underground rock. And if the buildout proceeds as planned, U.S. data centers alone could consume more natural gas than Germany and Japan combined by 2035. The reliance on natural gas also exposes hyperscalers to price fluctuations. One analyst expects that prices could more than triple by the end of the decade in some markets. If that happens, Anthropic might have a serious case of buyer’s remorse.

Show HN: DBDelve – Open-Source DB Client Made with Rust and GPUI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-09
16:36:38 UTC
01:36:38 KST

Hi HN, I’m Shayan and a few months ago I started building a DB Client DBDelve with a focus on performance and just making something that feels good to use (in the spirit of Zed, Ghostty, and other tools that just feel pleasant to use).
For my workflow I’ve always looked for performance, especially since some time ago I had a really outdated machine and any kind of bloat was really noticeable, I remember using DBeaver and it just crashing on me multiple times, I also had to use postGIS which just made it worse. I migrated all my essential dev tools to use the ones with performance in mind (Zed, Ghostty etc) but the only thing that was missing was DB Client. The main choices everyone has are DBeaver which is a memory hog and an overkill for most of the tasks imo. The other options like Datagrid, Beekeeper, TablePlus are either electron based so bloated and memory hogs or paid and closed-source.
DBDelve 0.3.6 against DBeaver 25.3.1 on the same Postgres table, median of 5 runs each (2026-10-11, M1 Pro, 32 GB). Times are from the action to the rows rendered.
                            DBDelve   DBeaver
  Launch                    1.1 s     5.2 s
  Idle memory               133 MB    606 MB
  1,000-row query           0.21 s    1.96 s
  1M rows, time             56 s      208 s
  1M rows, memory [1]       4.9 GB    17 GB
[1] The whole 1M-row, 100-column table pulled into memory on purpose, with the row limit off. Not a normal use case; DBeaver's heap limit had to be raised manually for the benchmark.
Scrolling perf with 1 million rows loaded with 100 columns each: https://youtu.be/V2MOhJYFqIE
It has most of the features most devs would need for 90% of their workflow plus some more I thought would be a nice touch:
Readonly, read-write and Full Access modes
Glass themes (If you’re into them, I am)
Keyboard focused with every keybinding customizable
Organization of connections into projects
Me and some other folks have been daily driving it for more than a month now and most good feedback comes on it having a really simple UI to navigate, very stable for its age and the performance of course. I’m also sharing here because those people tell me this has potential to grow so I’m trying my hand at distributing it.
Just want to give a huge shoutout here to the Zed team for GPUI, it's a breeze to work with if you just get through them not updating the crate officially on crates.io but the community has found the solutions for it, you just have to dig deep for it. It performs extremely well and just the HTML-like structure of it, makes it easy to understand for someone from a web dev background and agents are very good at writing it too. GPUI component also solves a lot of problems with having a good component library we can use. I think for anyone starting a GPUI project now, GPUI-kit makes a lot of sense, it just bundles GPUI, GPUI-component together and has some optimizations adding retained mode which is experimental but could provide a lot of benefit, so think all things considered it should be the default way.
The major optimization I did was just lowering the memory overhead by using packed rows which reduced the memory usage by 40% on large datasets (8.1GB to 4.9GB on a 4GB table loaded in app), everything else came bundled in with Rust and GPUI mostly or they just made it very easy.
Limitations:
It's not signed and notarized, identity verification from apple's side has been a nightmare but it should be signed soon.
Don’t expect feature parity with more mature clients for now, the general direction of this right now is the zed way of adding features in but after making sure the core workflows are done with a high quality.
Do give it a try, you can import your connections from dbeaver and tableplus.
https://github.com/ShayanAbbas1/dbdelve

Medium’s new TK app brings AI assistance directly into the writing process
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-09
16:12:28 UTC
01:12:28 KST

Online publishing platform Medium on Monday launched a new app, called TK, which aims to bring AI technology deeper into the writing process. The idea behind TK is to make it easier to turn ideas into written words by incorporating an AI assistant into the editor itself, allowing users to ask for help by typing “@TK” followed by their request or prompt.
In publishing and journalism, the term “TK” serves as a placeholder used to mark where missing information can be added later. The “TK” stands for “to come,” but uses a “K” instead of “C” as there are few English words where the “tk” letter combination exists, making it stand out more easily in written text where it could be caught by proofreaders.
In Medium’s app, TK takes on a new role as it tries to help users fill in the blanks.
The company suggests the AI assistant could help answer questions that you might normally have to switch to another tab to quickly look up, like how many days are in a particular month. The app could also pull in bits of writing you had previously saved to the app when you were still fleshing out your ideas.
In addition, Medium says TK will ship with particular skills for editorial feedback, headline feedback, and others that could match your draft to the style guide for Medium publications.
Medium’s move to embrace AI in the early stages of writing could prove controversial at a time when the publishing and literary worlds have been reckoning with the role that artificial intelligence has played in the creation of new long-form prose. Multiple authors have lost book deals over suspicions that they used AI technology to help them write, while other literary awards have come under scrutiny after winners were suspected of writing with AI assistance.
While writers have long used automated tools for proofreading and light grammatical edits, there is growing concern across the publishing industry that an AI assistant’s editorial “suggestions” can become the writing itself, instead of being reflective of the thoughts in the writer’s own mind.
But because AI models were trained on human writing, there are also questions around the reliability of AI detection tools in terms of their ability to properly determine when something was written with AI, rather than with its assistance, versus not at all.
TK leans into this debate, taking the side that these nuances will ultimately no longer matter in the end. Instead, the company celebrates what AI can bring to the world of writing, saying that “artificial intelligence makes writing more important, not less,” and proclaiming that “AI is a technology that has the power to amplify human intelligence and it uses the written word as a foundation.”
Still, Medium concedes that AI does raise the possibility of low-quality content and blurring the line between what’s human-written versus AI-written. To address these concerns, TK allows authors to publish notes that transparently explain how AI was used in their writing.
“This is a start of what we believe is required to publish in the AI era, which is to make the provenance of writing clear, transparent, and inspectable, right down to the prompting and source material,” Medium explained in a blog post about the launch.
In addition to writing assistance, TK will help users remember and organize what they had previously written and suggest writing prompts. The app can also optionally connect to your own AI agent through TK’s MCP server or Claude skill, so the app can better understand your projects, your positions, and other ideas that could be stored in your agent’s memory.
Meanwhile, the new app incorporates human feedback in a social layer, the company says, allowing writers to share their early drafts with others and get feedback.
At launch, TK is available on the web, but a desktop app is on the roadmap, Medium says. The app can import and export Markdown, but it’s not a Markdown app itself. The writing in TK is also not encrypted, as the app is designed for collaboration, but users will be able to set access control permissions on their work.
Medium, which is profitable, says TK will be a free tool for those with a Medium account.

Uber wants to park your car now, too
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-09
16:12:07 UTC
01:12:07 KST

Uber announced the launch of Uber Parking, a native in-app reservation feature that allows drivers to find, book, and pay for garage and lot spaces ahead of time. The new feature is a result of Uber’s recent acquisition of SpotHero, integrating a network of over 13,000 facilities across more than 400 cities into the company’s platform.
Uber wants to park your car now, too
Powered by its SpotHero acquisition, Uber’s new parking reservation tool is a play for commuter loyalty — and a staging ground for its robotaxi future.
The new feature works by tapping the new “Parking” icon in the Uber app to view an interactive map with upfront prices and arrival times. You can filter spots by self-park or valet, outdoor lot or garage, and whether staff are on-site. The app will prompt you to enter your vehicle details and license plate, after which can enter certain lots using a QR code on your phone or through an automatic license plate scan. If your plans change, you can extend your time directly in the app or cancel for free right up until your reservation starts.
Uber One subscribers can earn 10 percent back on parking reservations as account credits within 24 hours. These credits can then be spent on rides or Uber Eats deliveries. Uber says that its subscription service has grown to more than 55 million members across 47 countries as of late 2026.
Uber Parking is launching in 15 initial markets, including Chicago, NYC, Boston, San Francisco, Los Angeles, Washington D.C., Atlanta, Austin, Dallas, Denver, Miami, Nashville, Philadelphia, San Diego, and Seattle — eventually rolling out to SpotHero’s existing 400-city footprint.
The move also ties directly into Uber’s wider bet on robotaxis, working with over 30 autonomous vehicle partners across multiple cities. In the long run, these 13,000-plus parking facilities won’t just hold commuter cars — Uber plans to turn them into urban holding pens and waiting areas for driverless robotaxis.
Stashing autonomous fleets off the street when demand dips helps keep empty cars from aimlessly circling city blocks, cutting down on traffic, emissions, and wear on the vehicles, Uber says. Ultimately, it shows that the company is thinking bigger than just ride-hailing and delivery — it wants to control the city’s physical roads and parking spaces, regardless of whether the person traveling is driving their own car, riding in the backseat, or letting a computer take the wheel.
By getting into parking, Uber is also tacitly admitting that its earlier mission to end personal car ownership and driver’s licenses didn’t succeed. But there is a loyalty-retaining strategy at play here, too, with Uber intent on keeping its customers operating within in its own platform ecosystem, whether they’re hailing a ride or driving their own car.

More than 400k Russians killed fighting in Ukraine war, leaked data suggests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-09
16:11:00 UTC
01:11:00 KST

More than 400,000 Russians have been killed fighting in Ukraine since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion nearly five years ago, according to data leaked from the state statistics agency, Rosstat.
The information, obtained by the Belarusian opposition-linked hacker group Cyber Partisans and the Ukrainian hacking collective Silent Crow, contains more than 11m death certificates, including details of the deceased’s age, place of residence and location of death.
It was later shared with the Guardian and a small group of other media outlets.
According to the data, 412,576 death certificates explicitly linked the fatalities to the war, either through official cause-of-death codes or written references to combat and military operations.
The figures underscore the staggering human toll of Russia’s war against Ukraine, with no end in sight despite a fresh round of peace talks scheduled to take place in Abu Dhabi this week.
The two hacking groups announced the breach on 1 November and published the data over the weekend. Rosstat confirmed it had been hacked but denied that any sensitive information had been obtained.
The dataset offers an unprecedentedly detailed picture of Russia’s wartime losses, which Moscow has sought to conceal. The Russian authorities have not published a death toll since the early months of the invasion, and information about military casualties is treated as a state secret.
The Guardian could not independently verify the authenticity of the entire dataset. However, the figures are broadly consistent with other estimates of Russian losses. British intelligence in September estimated that about 500,000 Russian soldiers had been killed since the start of the invasion.
Separately, the independent Russian outlet Mediazona has identified by name nearly 286,000 Russian military personnel killed in Ukraine, drawing on official records, social media obituaries and photographs of gravestones. The outlet estimates the true toll is closer to half a million.
“The data looks authentic, and it’s very rich,” said Janis Kluge, the head of the Russia and Eurasia division at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs.
“This is the biggest leak of data when it comes to Russian casualties,” added Kluge, who has studied Russian war statistics extensively.
The dataset is likely to underestimate the true death toll. Some soldiers remain missing, while others have never been identified.
Kluge also pointed to a significant delay between deaths occurring and being entered into official records, which he said typically took about six months.
“We are probably at this time closer to 500,000 killed Russian soldiers than 400,000,” he said.
The figures also reveal the unequal burden of the war across Russia, with poorer and more remote regions sustaining disproportionately heavy losses.
In Buryatia, Tuva and Zabaykalsky Krai, three regions in eastern Russia, war-related fatalities accounted for about a third of all deaths among men aged 18 to 49 between the start of the invasion and mid-2024. In Moscow and St Petersburg, the equivalent figure was about 10%.
There was also a sharp rise in Russian battlefield deaths as the war dragged on, with some of the deadliest months coming in late 2024 and 2025.
Kluge, who has been analysing the data, said the number of soldiers killed in several months during that period exceeded 15,000, equivalent to roughly 500 a day.
“In late 2024 and in 2025, you see that the numbers in many months are above 15,000 per month, and that’s higher than I think most estimates were,” Kluge said. “That’s 500 a day, above 500 a day. Certainly shocking.”
The scale of the losses is staggering by any measure and unprecedented in Russia’s modern history.
In less than five years, Russian military deaths in Ukraine are estimated to have exceeded the combined death toll from all Soviet and Russian wars between the end of the second world war and the start of the full-scale invasion more than eightfold. The figure also exceeds the number of US military personnel who died during the second world war.
Rather than push Moscow towards a settlement, the scale of the losses is likely to harden Vladimir Putin’s resolve, according to a person familiar with the Russian president’s thinking.
“Putin understands these numbers, and for him to now settle for anything less than everything he wants would feel like a betrayal of himself and the people,” the person said.
Senior Russian and Ukrainian negotiators are due to meet in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday for the first US-brokered peace talks between them in nine months.
Previous negotiations have made little progress towards ending the war, with Moscow demanding that Ukraine withdraw from the parts of the Donbas region it still controls.
Neither Putin nor his Ukrainian counterpart, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, will attend the talks. Instead, both countries will send senior delegations, with Donald Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner also expected to take part.
In a post on X, Witkoff said the negotiations would focus on “post-war security arrangement, de-escalation” and humanitarian issues.
European governments have expressed concern that the talks could extend beyond Ukraine to broader questions of European security, including Moscow’s longstanding demands for a reduction of Nato’s military presence in countries bordering Russia.
France’s foreign minister said Paris would participate in the negotiations but the Kremlin subsequently denied that France would be represented.

Payments Canada announces launch of Canada's Real-Time Rail (RTR) payment system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-09
16:00:45 UTC
01:00:45 KST

Canada launches the Real-Time Rail, bringing 24/7 payment infrastructure to the national economy
The new system will enable participating financial service providers to clear and settle payments in real time, providing a made-in-Canada platform for future innovation and prosperity.
OTTAWA, ON, November 9, 2026 – Payments Canada today announced the launch of Canada’s Real-Time Rail (RTR). This new national payment system will transform day-to-day payments for Canadian businesses and consumers by enabling instant speed and settlement, real-time cash-flow visibility and data-rich messaging through existing banking and payment channels.
The launch of Canada’s RTR marks a major milestone in modernizing the critical infrastructure that underpins Canada’s economy and future growth. The RTR will enable participating members, including financial institutions, credit unions and payment service providers, to exchange, clear and settle payments securely in real time for their customers, 24 hours a day, every day of the year.
“A stronger, more productive economy relies on modern financial infrastructure that can match our ambition,” said the Honourable François-Philippe Champagne, Minister of Finance and National Revenue. “The launch of Canada’s Real-Time Rail lays the foundation for a more dynamic and competitive digital economy, driving innovation, expanding choice and creating new opportunities for Canadians while positioning our country for long-term growth.”
“The launch of Canada’s Real-Time Rail marks the beginning of a new era for payments in our country,” said Susan E. Hawkins, President and CEO, Payments Canada. “As a national asset that’s designed specifically for our country, the RTR gives the payment ecosystem a modern foundation to build on. By collectively leveraging this rail, our ecosystem will unleash its full potential, enabling our members to build capabilities that drive innovation, resilience and growth for businesses and consumers across the nation.”
Ron Morrow, the Honourable François-Philippe Champagne and Susan E. Hawkins
The RTR will drive significant cost savings and economic growth in Canada over the next decade. The C.D. Howe Institute projects that, with its functionalities at launch, the RTR will generate up to $14.5 billion in cost savings from lower processing costs, reduced use of cash and cheques, and reduced float (the period during which funds are temporarily unavailable to the recipient). Extending beyond these cost savings, the RTR is expected to generate $16 billion in economic gains, growing to $27 billion as new functionalities are introduced over time.
“The Real-Time Rail is an important step in modernizing Canada's payment infrastructure and ensuring it keeps pace with Canadians' evolving needs,” said Tiff Macklem, Governor of the Bank of Canada. “The Bank will oversee the system so that it operates safely and reliably while ensuring Canadians can benefit from innovations in financial services.”
Owned and operated by Payments Canada, and built in collaboration with delivery partners CGI, Deloitte Canada, IBM Canada and Interac Corp., the RTR leverages ISO 20022 data-rich messaging. Through this shared technical language, the RTR holds the potential to strengthen Canada’s economic sovereign autonomy and support its global competitiveness.
Fraud safeguards from day one
Canada is the first G7 country to deploy a real-time payment system with mandatory centralized fraud services for use at launch. These services will be used alongside participants’ existing fraud controls to mitigate the risk of fraud for Canadian businesses and consumers at multiple levels. Fraud controls required at the launch of Canada’s RTR include:
- Confirmation of payee (available for consumer accounts on day one)
- A fraud transaction “safety” score
- A risk list or repository of fraud risks and indicators
- A fraud reporting and intelligence platform
While no system is entirely immune to risk, these measures establish a strong, coordinated layer of defence across the payment network.
At-launch member participants
The initial cohort of active RTR system participants includes:
- Wealthsimple
- Questbank
- Peoples Trust Company
- Paramount Commerce
- KOHO
- DoBusiness.com™
- Digital Commerce Bank
- Bank of America
Canada’s deliberately sequenced RTR rollout pairs day-one security with rapid scalability. With additional participants onboarding continually in the coming months, including all major Canadian financial institutions and other members applying for access, the RTR will be available to more than nine in 10 Canadians within the first year after launch.
Made-in Canada, for Canada
The launch of the RTR reflects our ‘Team Canada’ approach, bringing together regulators, members, stakeholders and delivery partners around a shared vision. Built in Canada and designed to serve all Canadians, the RTR provides accessible payment infrastructure through existing banking and payment channels. This infrastructure supports a diverse country and a broad range of communities, including small businesses, newcomers and people in rural areas.
Payments Canada research found that 60 per cent of Canadian businesses are ready to adopt real-time payments to address everyday challenges such as forecasting cash flow and waiting to send and receive funds. More than half of surveyed consumers (52 per cent) also expressed interest and intent to use real-time payments.
To meet this evolving need, the RTR serves as a secure platform for innovation. With it, system participants can build and offer products and services that benefit consumers and businesses across the country, supporting a changing economy and Canada's future prosperity.
An infrastructure for the future
Canada’s Real-Time Rail is an important step toward a more productive, innovative and inclusive economy, and the work will continue to ensure the country’s payment infrastructure meets Canadians’ evolving needs.
Learn more about Canada’s Real-Time Rail

About Payments Canada
Payments Canada enables prosperity, productivity and safety for Canada through trusted, critical national payment infrastructure. As a public-purpose organization, we own and operate: Lynx, our high-value payment system; the Automated Clearing Settlement System (ACSS), our retail batch payment system; and the Real-Time Rail (RTR), our new real-time payment system. We establish the by-laws, rules and standards that govern these systems, which cleared and settled $103 trillion in 2025 — more than $411 billion every business day. Transactions that pass through our systems include debit card payments, pre-authorized debits, direct deposits, bill payments, wire payments and cheques. In collaboration with our diverse membership, we continue to modernize Canada’s payment ecosystem to promote innovation, competition and deliver efficiencies that power a modern economy.
For media inquiries, please visit Payments Canada’s media centre.

About Payments Canada
Payments Canada enables prosperity, productivity and safety for Canada through trusted, critical national payment infrastructure. As a public-purpose organization, we own and operate: Lynx, our high-value payment system; the Automated Clearing Settlement System (ACSS), our retail batch payment system; and the Real-Time Rail (RTR), our new real-time payment system. We establish the by-laws, rules and standards that govern these systems, which cleared and settled $103 trillion in 2025 — more than $411 billion every business day. Transactions that pass through our systems include debit card payments, pre-authorized debits, direct deposits, bill payments, wire payments and cheques. In collaboration with our diverse membership, we continue to modernize Canada’s payment ecosystem to promote innovation, competition and deliver efficiencies that power a modern economy.
For media inquiries, please visit Payments Canada’s media centre.

Reddit Founder Says Building Social Media Apps Is 'Not Cool Anymore'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-09
16:00:00 UTC
01:00:00 KST

Reddit Founder Says Building Social Media Apps Is 'Not Cool Anymore' (wired.com) 38
			
		 	
				An anonymous reader quotes a report from Wired: Alexis Ohanian wants to figure out the future of user-generated content. According to the Reddit cofounder, building social media apps is "not cool anymore" and so much of the internet has been compromised. "I'm expecting some better version of the group chat to be that new version of UGC," Ohanian told WIRED senior correspondent Lauren Goode at the inaugural WIRED World Fair. [...] Ohanian is a proponent of the "Dead Internet Theory"—the idea that a lot of online activity and content is being generated by bots. Large language models have turbocharged this, with AI agents outrunning human users. "The internet that I grew up on  that was really built for humans first; user interfaces and experiences are going to go away," said Ohanian, "because more of the internet is going to get created for these agents to use, [rather] than for people."
In some ways, the advance in generative AI has been lucrative for sites like Reddit, which has licensed its vast archive of human conversations to companies including Google and OpenAI to train AI models. "Platforms like ours became very, very valuable to LLMs," Ohanian said. But the technology has also undermined the business. Reddit shares plunged 29 percent last week after the platform warned that Google's AI-powered search was hurting referral traffic. Ohanian also worries the commercialization of these conversations means they are full of "bullshit." "The internet has gotten so manipulated because it is so incredibly valuable to do so," he said.
Reddit recently said it would require users to sign in to fight third-party scraping and keep up user engagement. While Ohanian declined to say whether he agrees with the move, "there has to be provable humanity on the internet without being creepy."  An early Anthropic investor, Ohanian is nonetheless optimistic about the potential benefits of AI. He is especially excited to see medical breakthroughs from the technology. "There is still a very real chance that this technology can cause a lot of harm for sure," he said. "I think we have to be sober about how we're building and what we're doing, but I still can't help but see all of the things that can get so demonstrably better."

Asked about AI executives’ warnings about their models’ safety on 60 Minutes, Trump said, “I think that the risk is not nearly as real as it– as they talk, and I think the risk can be managed, and it’s managed.” He claimed the DOJ is managing that risk, saying, “We had a situation where somebody was reported to us to be doing something bad with AI. Trump’s 60 Minutes interview touched on AI safety, threat to arrest an AI exec
Trump claims the DOJ told a top AI executive, ‘get ready to go to jail.’
Trump refused to name the person or company he was referring to, but said it was the leader of an AI company, “One of the big ones.” He claimed that after the threat of arrest, “this person totally changed everything.” Despite previously claiming that “artificial intelligence” is a term used by people he considers the enemy, Trump said AI rather than SI or super intelligence multiple times during the interview. We’re leading number one. And China has no guardrails, by the way. [...] They have the guardrails that whatever President Xi says goes. With me, it’s pretty strong, but it’s not quite that strong.”

The same H100 costs $2.69 or $12.29 an hour depending where you rent it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-09
15:39:01 UTC
00:39:01 KST

On-demand GPU rental prices across AWS, Azure and the neoclouds, normalised to dollars per GPU per hour and grouped so only identical GPUs are compared.
4.57× between cheapest and dearest, for the same chip. One GPU running continuously for a month is $1,964 or $8,972 depending only on where you rent it.
"An H100" is three different products. The SXM 80GB, the PCIe 80GB and the NVL 94GB all get marketed as H100s and they do not cost the same. Putting them in one chart manufactures a spread that isn't there, so every comparison here is within a single (model, memory) group.
The same applies within a vendor: Azure lists the same A100 PCIe 80GB at one, two and four GPUs per VM for $3.67, $4.78 and $4.78 per GPU-hour. The spread uses each vendor's cheapest route to a given GPU, so an Azure-vs-Azure gap never shows up as a market gap. RunPod Secure and Community are counted as one company.
It is not pure margin. Going from Azure's ND series to RunPod Community gives up:
- InfiniBand. Azure's ND SKU has 400 Gbps per GPU of Quantum-2 InfiniBand with GPU Direct RDMA, which is what makes multi-node training work. That is the reason the ND series is priced above Azure's own single-H100 NC SKU ($6.98).
- A datacentre SLA. RunPod Community is third-party hosts renting out their own hardware.
- Enterprise compliance, committed capacity, and the rest of the hyperscaler surface.
If you are fine-tuning on one node, you are paying for an interconnect you will never use. If you are training across 64 nodes, the cheap row is not an option.
python3 collect.py   # ~1 GB AWS index, slow
python3 compute.py
- On-demand list prices only. Reserved, committed-use and spot pricing all cut the hyperscaler numbers, and spot in particular would narrow the gap a lot.
- Single region each (AWS us-east-1, Azure eastus).
- GPU counts come from vendor documentation, not from the price label — AWS
reports "640 GB HBM3" for a p5 and Azure reports an accelerator-memory total,
and neither states a per-GPU model. Doc URLs are in compare.json.
- Lambda is excluded from the headline spread. Its published page states the listed rates take effect 2026-11-16; current rates are behind a login. Its rows are shown separately and labelled.
- Availability is not priced. A cheap H100 you cannot get is not a price.

The Walt Disney Company has teamed up with Adobe to develop proprietary “artist-led” generative AI models to support Disney’s production pipeline. The multiyear partnership was announced today at Adobe’s MAX conference, and it will see Adobe providing Disney with early access to its latest technologies for everything from Disney’s theme parks and cruise line to ESPN content. Disney and Adobe will also collaborate “to explore emerging technologies, including responsibly developed AI,” according to Adobe’s press release:
Disney and Adobe are building generative AI tools together
The partnership will give Disney ‘early access’ to AI tech for its resorts, cruise line, ESPN graphics, and more.
With Adobe Firefly Foundry, Disney will work directly with Adobe on generative AI models tailored to Disney’s properties that are human-centered and artist-led. Customized on Disney properties, these proprietary models are trained on unique world knowledge (character attributes, environments, visual styles) to generate commercially safe and production-ready outputs, while accelerating work and enabling the development of more creative projects.
The announcement builds on the existing relationship between the two companies, with Adobe noting that Disney’s Imagineering R&D division is already using the Firefly AI platform for theme park development. Adobe will contribute to “expand internal creative workflows” at Walt Disney Studios and identify how AI can be used to shape ESPN content and “enhance the engagement with sports fans.”
This is the latest example of Disney embracing generative AI tools, following a previous deal with OpenAI and involvement with Character.AI’s bankruptcy. Bloomberg reported last week that Disney is gearing up to lay off thousands of staffers and targeting 20 percent annual cost savings, in what’s expected to be its fourth round of job cuts in 2026.

Meta expands Instagram’s AI age-guessing tech globally
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-09
15:32:27 UTC
00:32:27 KST

Meta announced on Monday that it’s expanding its AI-powered age-estimation technology on Instagram worldwide to identify more teens and place them under its Teen Account protections, as it faces numerous lawsuits accusing its platforms of harming teens.
The social media giant says it will use the AI technology to find people it suspects to be teens, even if they use an adult birthday.
Teen Accounts place users into a stricter account experience with additional safeguards, such as receiving direct messages only from people they follow or are already connected to, hiding harmful comments, and setting accounts to private by default.
Meta’s age-guessing tools use AI to analyze entire profiles for contextual clues, such as birthday celebrations or mentions of school grades. Meta also looks for these signals across different formats, such as posts, comments, bios, captions, and more. The company also looks at visual cues from photos and videos, including a person’s height or bone structure.
Meta said it’s continuing to roll out the technology on Facebook, with a similar global rollout planned for Threads later this year.
The global expansion comes as Meta reached settlements worth up to $18 billion with nearly every U.S. state and territory in August to resolve lawsuits alleging its platforms harm teens. As part of the settlements, Meta agreed to improve how it identifies teens and children under 13.
“We’ll continue to do our part to proactively ensure teens are in age-appropriate experiences on our apps,” Meta wrote in a blog post. “That’s why as part of our agreement with 52 bipartisan attorneys general across US states, territories, and the District of Columbia, we’re investing in even stronger technology to proactively catch accounts that may belong to children under 13. We’re also strengthening the technology we use to identify accounts that may belong to teens between the ages of 13 and 17 so we can ensure those accounts are placed in experiences designed for teens, even if they give us an adult birthday.”
Meta said parents in the U.S. will start seeing an in-feed video on Instagram explaining its approach to ensuring their teens are in age-appropriate protections.

Waymo robotaxis kept illegally passing school buses after software fix, feds say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-09
15:24:59 UTC
00:24:59 KST

Nearly a year ago, Waymo updated its self-driving software and issued a recall after numerous reports that its robotaxis were illegally passing school buses that had stopped and deployed flashing red lights. Now, federal safety regulators have opened a new investigation into why that behavior has continued.
The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) said in a November 6 filing that a majority of these reported incidents occurred after the company deployed a software update intended to fix the problem.
Reuters was the first to report the filing.
Waymo said last year that a software update was completed for all affected vehicles on November 17, 2025. However, NHTSA said the majority of the incidents occurred after the software update. NHTSA’s Office of Defects Investigation (ODI) has opened a “recall query” to “assess the adequacy of the remedy.”
The ODI opened its initial investigation into Waymo in October 2025 after seeing footage of one of its autonomous vehicles maneuvering around a stopped school bus that had its stop sign extended, lights flashing, and was unloading children in Atlanta. In that incident, a Waymo robotaxi crossed perpendicularly in front of the school bus from its right side. The autonomous vehicle then turned left around the front of the bus before traveling down the street.
Numerous other incidents have been documented in the weeks and months since in Austin, where Waymo also operates a robotaxi service. Austin Independent School District officials reported at least five such incidents at the time, according to a letter filed with NHTSA.
Reached for comment, Waymo stressed the importance of safety to its mission. “We have made significant improvements to vehicle behavior around school buses and have received no citations since March 2026,” a spokesperson told TechCrunch via email. “The Waymo Driver has a clearly demonstrated positive impact on roadway safety. Once received, we’ll work to respond to NHTSA’s query and look forward to continuing our engagement on recall processes for AV software that continues to learn and improve.”
TechCrunch also reached out to Austin Independent School District officials for comment and will update the article if they respond.
This article was updated after publication with Waymo’s statement.

Crypto foundation demanded employees endorse suicide pledge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-09
15:23:57 UTC
00:23:57 KST

On a Friday in March, employees at an international technology foundation received a 38-page document outlining leadership’s vision for the foundation for the next 1,000 years.
The document went out to all employees of The Ethereum Foundation, a nonprofit organization registered in Switzerland that supports Ethereum, a popular cryptocurrency platform and the second-largest blockchain network in the world, valued at about $300 billion, according to a federal lawsuit filed by a Boulder resident Wednesday in U.S. District Court for the District of Colorado.
Titled “The Ethereum Foundation Mandate,” the document featured ethereal illustrated scenes of glowing lights and anime-style characters voyaging through dark forests. The pages featured white text against a navy blue background and were adorned with cartoon flowers, rainbows and diamonds.
And on page 11 — nestled between a winking anime woman and three yellow cats — was a suicide pledge.
Authors, maintainers, editors and distributors of “this software” would pledge to ensure the software remained free and publicly accessible, and would also vow to “take his or her own life with a sword upon failure to uphold any of the pledges in this license,” the illustration read. It was labeled “Source Seppuku License,” an apparent reference to a traditional Japanese ritual suicide.
When the document went out on that Friday in March, employees were told to commit to the principles in the mandate by Monday or quit their jobs, according to the lawsuit brought by Kayleen Fulton, a Boulder woman who was fired from the Ethereum Foundation after she led employee resistance to the suicide pledge.
Employees were to return a form with one of two options checked, according to a copy of the document included in legal filings.
Choice one: “I personally commit to the direction set out in the mandate, I commit to help translate it into thoroughly reasoned strategies for my domain, and I commit to an exclusive and energetic focus on the mission-critical tasks necessary for its implementation. From today and until my last day at the EF.”
Or choice two: “I cannot confidently commit to the above and would like to request my extra months of compensation and leave the EF without undue delay.”
An email to the foundation seeking comment on this story was not immediately returned Thursday, but a foundation leader at the time told employees the suicide pledge was not meant to be taken literally, according to the lawsuit. After employee pushback, managers updated the commitment form to clarify that the form had “nothing to do with literal seppuku,” according to the lawsuit.
Resistance to the suicide pledge was swift and vocal, and began when the Ethereum Foundation’s board put out a draft of the mandate to staff in late February, Fulton alleged in the lawsuit. Employees soon asked whether they were pledging to die by suicide and wondered in workplace forums whether the pledge was a test of their loyalty to Ethereum’s core principles. One employee referenced a colleague’s recent death by suicide.
“I have a new hire joining tomorrow,” another employee wrote in a discussion about the suicide pledge, according to the lawsuit. “The first thing he’s going to see… is a motion to drop a clause that mandates employees commit the ultimate sacrifice by falling on a sword.”
Nearly 80 of the foundation’s 250 or so employees voted to nix the suicide pledge after the draft was released, according to the lawsuit, but leadership at the Ethereum Foundation ignored their objections and included the pledge word-for-word in the final version of the mandate. The final published version presented the suicide pledge in an illustration instead of including it in the main body of the mandate, as it had been in the draft version.
The mandate’s visual aesthetic — the anime and other illustrations — reflected imagery from a controversial online figure who was known to promote “white nationalist ideology and disturbing pro-anorexia content,” according to the lawsuit.
When an Ethereum Foundation board member objected to the aesthetic, Ethereum founder Vitalik Buterin responded that “the controversialness (sic) of those aesthetics is itself part of the point,” according to the lawsuit.
After demanding that employees agree to the mandate, Bastian Aue, co-executive director of the Ethereum Foundation, defended the suicide pledge to employees as “part of the artwork of the mandate.”
It was, he said, “a cultural reference like other elements in there. Chosen deliberately, but not meant to be taken literally.”
In the days after the mandate was pushed out to employees, Fulton and a colleague organized and sent the foundation’s board a letter in which 53 employees endorsed the mandate’s general direction but declined to return the commitment form. The employees also declined to resign, according to the lawsuit.
Aue ultimately allowed the letter-signers to keep their jobs. But he fired Fulton and her colleague who helped organize the letter. Buterin later told Fulton — who had just been diagnosed with cancer — that the firing was about company dynamics, according to the lawsuit.
“If you reward making a stink with outcomes, then everyone will know that essentially making that kind of show both internally and externally is the way to cause outcomes inside of the EF,” he said, according to the lawsuit, which cited a recorded conversation between the pair.
The mandate started an exodus at the Ethereum Foundation, according to the lawsuit. The board member who’d objected to the mandate’s visual aesthetics started a sabbatical the day Fulton was fired and resigned in June. By September, eight senior employees had left, according to the lawsuit, and most of the 53 people who signed the letter had resigned or been terminated.
Fulton, who had earned a salary of $195,000 in her role at the Ethereum Foundation, sued for disability discrimination, retaliation, interference with her rights under the Family and Medical Leave Act, unfair employment practices and related claims. Her lawsuit notes that the Ethereum Foundation “does not hire or pay its United States staff in its own name,” but instead uses employer-of-record service companies.
One of her attorneys, James Bartolomei, declined to comment Thursday, saying the lawsuit spoke for itself.

Crypto foundation demanded employees endorse suicide pledge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-09
15:23:57 UTC
00:23:57 KST

On a Friday in March, employees at an international technology foundation received a 38-page document outlining leadership’s vision for the foundation for the next 1,000 years.
The document went out to all employees of The Ethereum Foundation, a nonprofit organization registered in Switzerland that supports Ethereum, a popular cryptocurrency platform and the second-largest blockchain network in the world, valued at about $300 billion, according to a federal lawsuit filed by a Boulder resident Wednesday in U.S. District Court for the District of Colorado.
Titled “The Ethereum Foundation Mandate,” the document featured ethereal illustrated scenes of glowing lights and anime-style characters voyaging through dark forests. The pages featured white text against a navy blue background and were adorned with cartoon flowers, rainbows and diamonds.
And on page 11 — nestled between a winking anime woman and three yellow cats — was a suicide pledge.
Authors, maintainers, editors and distributors of “this software” would pledge to ensure the software remained free and publicly accessible, and would also vow to “take his or her own life with a sword upon failure to uphold any of the pledges in this license,” the illustration read. It was labeled “Source Seppuku License,” an apparent reference to a traditional Japanese ritual suicide.
When the document went out on that Friday in March, employees were told to commit to the principles in the mandate by Monday or quit their jobs, according to the lawsuit brought by Kayleen Fulton, a Boulder woman who was fired from the Ethereum Foundation after she led employee resistance to the suicide pledge.
Employees were to return a form with one of two options checked, according to a copy of the document included in legal filings.
Choice one: “I personally commit to the direction set out in the mandate, I commit to help translate it into thoroughly reasoned strategies for my domain, and I commit to an exclusive and energetic focus on the mission-critical tasks necessary for its implementation. From today and until my last day at the EF.”
Or choice two: “I cannot confidently commit to the above and would like to request my extra months of compensation and leave the EF without undue delay.”
An email to the foundation seeking comment on this story was not immediately returned Thursday, but a foundation leader at the time told employees the suicide pledge was not meant to be taken literally, according to the lawsuit. After employee pushback, managers updated the commitment form to clarify that the form had “nothing to do with literal seppuku,” according to the lawsuit.
Resistance to the suicide pledge was swift and vocal, and began when the Ethereum Foundation’s board put out a draft of the mandate to staff in late February, Fulton alleged in the lawsuit. Employees soon asked whether they were pledging to die by suicide and wondered in workplace forums whether the pledge was a test of their loyalty to Ethereum’s core principles. One employee referenced a colleague’s recent death by suicide.
“I have a new hire joining tomorrow,” another employee wrote in a discussion about the suicide pledge, according to the lawsuit. “The first thing he’s going to see… is a motion to drop a clause that mandates employees commit the ultimate sacrifice by falling on a sword.”
Nearly 80 of the foundation’s 250 or so employees voted to nix the suicide pledge after the draft was released, according to the lawsuit, but leadership at the Ethereum Foundation ignored their objections and included the pledge word-for-word in the final version of the mandate. The final published version presented the suicide pledge in an illustration instead of including it in the main body of the mandate, as it had been in the draft version.
The mandate’s visual aesthetic — the anime and other illustrations — reflected imagery from a controversial online figure who was known to promote “white nationalist ideology and disturbing pro-anorexia content,” according to the lawsuit.
When an Ethereum Foundation board member objected to the aesthetic, Ethereum founder Vitalik Buterin responded that “the controversialness (sic) of those aesthetics is itself part of the point,” according to the lawsuit.
After demanding that employees agree to the mandate, Bastian Aue, co-executive director of the Ethereum Foundation, defended the suicide pledge to employees as “part of the artwork of the mandate.”
It was, he said, “a cultural reference like other elements in there. Chosen deliberately, but not meant to be taken literally.”
In the days after the mandate was pushed out to employees, Fulton and a colleague organized and sent the foundation’s board a letter in which 53 employees endorsed the mandate’s general direction but declined to return the commitment form. The employees also declined to resign, according to the lawsuit.
Aue ultimately allowed the letter-signers to keep their jobs. But he fired Fulton and her colleague who helped organize the letter. Buterin later told Fulton — who had just been diagnosed with cancer — that the firing was about company dynamics, according to the lawsuit.
“If you reward making a stink with outcomes, then everyone will know that essentially making that kind of show both internally and externally is the way to cause outcomes inside of the EF,” he said, according to the lawsuit, which cited a recorded conversation between the pair.
The mandate started an exodus at the Ethereum Foundation, according to the lawsuit. The board member who’d objected to the mandate’s visual aesthetics started a sabbatical the day Fulton was fired and resigned in June. By September, eight senior employees had left, according to the lawsuit, and most of the 53 people who signed the letter had resigned or been terminated.
Fulton, who had earned a salary of $195,000 in her role at the Ethereum Foundation, sued for disability discrimination, retaliation, interference with her rights under the Family and Medical Leave Act, unfair employment practices and related claims. Her lawsuit notes that the Ethereum Foundation “does not hire or pay its United States staff in its own name,” but instead uses employer-of-record service companies.
One of her attorneys, James Bartolomei, declined to comment Thursday, saying the lawsuit spoke for itself.

Today, I’m talking with Mitch Glazier, who is CEO and chairman of the RIAA.
Hold up — I had a great time talking to the RIAA guy
This time around, RIAA CEO Mitch Glazier and music fans are fighting on the same side.
This conversation was a real full-circle moment for me: I was in college when Napster hit, and the RIAA became everyone’s villain for suing kids for downloading music. That was when I decided to go be a copyright lawyer, which set the rest of my career in motion — and Mitch was in the background as a young lawyer at the RIAA working on those cases. That’s because here in 2026, Mitch, the RIAA, the record labels, the artists, and ordinary people are all pretty unhappy with the big AI companies in the same way, for training on everyone’s work without permission and flooding our feeds with slop.
Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here.
Everyone is mad about it! It didn’t feel like it at the time for me. Thank you for saying the butterfly effect is real. But it was heated. It was hot.

It feels like I’m just giving up all of the ideals that I had when I was a kid about the internet, that open access to information was good, that... Some of it has been because of the democratization of the industry, where the gatekeeping roles have changed, where the partnerships between those who partner and invest with artists and the artists themselves have changed. In a world where artists and label services, like à la carte services, are a bigger part of revenue, in an area where catalog, forever exploitation, and new investors in the industry have come in, the landscape is much wider now. Now there are dozens of different types of folks meeting artists in different places where they are and meeting fans in different places where they are. The good news is, unlike Napster, I don’t feel like we are facing it at odds, which is kind of what it felt like back then. And to me, we’re not fighting in this space anymore between just a business model or an investment. We are now fighting to keep the art as human and the connection between an artist and a fan preserved and alive. And that to me just seems like a much larger purpose, I guess. So it feels very different to me. It feels like a good bookend.
Like you, I started my career with Napster, but I was on the other side, learned a ton as a young lawyer, and now on the other side, we have AI, and comparing the two is so wild. So there’s even less scarcity because you can just horsepower an AI pop star into existence singing an AI song, and there’s going to be a glut of supply.

So obviously the RIAA is well known; it’s either a hero or a villain, depending on where you are in your story, as we have both determined.
Tell people what the RIAA is, how big it is, and how it’s structured.
We’re based in Washington, D.C., because that’s where the federal government is. We used to be based in New York. RIAA actually started as a tech standards association. They created the RIAA curve, the equalization curve that allowed both the recording and the playback of vinyl records in a way that would work on every single record player. So it didn’t really start out as a lobbying organization or a litigation organization; that’s how we became famous or infamous, depending on where you sit. We started out as a tech standards organization, and we still do that. We still participate in international standard-setting organizations right now to try to set the fields, for example, for the metadata that people will use, whether it’s AI or any other technological format, or in labeling, for example. But we also run the gold and platinum program, which we’re probably best known for with the general public.
So we’re like those nerdy auditors that actually certify the gold and platinum records, like the PricewaterhouseCoopers lawyers that walk out on the Oscars or whatever. But that’s great because it allows us to interact directly with artists and celebrate their success, which is very cool. We also put together all the revenue from the entire recorded part of the music business, and we release that twice a year. That helps inform people about the markets, and it helps to, on the business side, give people the benchmarks that they need industry-wide. Everybody knows what their company is doing, what their management company is doing, but to know what the whole industry is doing and whether or not you are on par is quite helpful.
We are the spokesperson when the industry is aligned. We’re out there talking on behalf of the industry. We technically represent the major labels, but we forge coalitions because whether you’re major or indie, whether you’re an artist or a publisher or a songwriter, most of the time our interests are aligned. Every once in a while we fight with each other, but when we are aligned, which I would say is 90 percent of the time, the RIAA is sort of the driving force in building coalitions so that we can all speak together.
So we do a lot of stuff. We don’t just sue people and lobby the government, although those are big parts of what we do. And then we also take on the content protection force for the industry. Our content protection department operates 365 days per year, 24 hours per day. We work with sister organizations in London and New Zealand. So it doesn’t matter what time of day it is; we have people coordinated and working around the clock. And then we do all those take-down notices. We get a note from a manager saying, “A pre-release of this artist’s material that hasn’t come out yet is up. We need your help getting it down.”
We do all of that, and we do it... The entire organization is only 46 people.
Wow.
Isn’t that amazing? But the most passionate music lovers you would ever imagine.
It’s only 46 people?
Only 46 people.
How is that structured? Does everyone just do everything all day long?
There aren’t as many redundancies as there should be. We’re divided into those different departments, like content protection, communications and research, public policy and industry relations, and obviously legal affairs. So we are, I would say, small and nimble, but we punch above our weight. We are high profile, but our industry, if you think about it compared to the folks that we are up against, if you want to view it that way, is really small. I mean, the entire recorded music business was $11 billion wholesale last year in the United States. The market cap of just one AI company is $2 trillion.
So when we are out there lobbying, and we’ve got our three-person lobbying team at the RIAA trying to make a point to policymakers, and you’re dealing with super PAC money that equals $250 million in a midterm cycle, we don’t have that kind of revenue. But what we do have is music, and we have artists who everybody loves, who are culture makers, and who are messengers that people trust and listen to. I think we do pretty well for our tininess.
The other question I ask every CEO who comes on the show is about decisions. You have a lot of decisions to make. Some of these are decisions of first impression. No one has ever decided how AI and art should work together. How do you make decisions? What’s your framework?
Personally, my leadership style is that I like to have people around me who are not “yes” people. I don’t want people just sort of... If I come up with an idea, I don’t want it to be reinforced immediately. If you agree with that, great. But I like to hear from everybody. I think my team knows that I like to hear the truth, and I want to hear their raw opinion because I want to check my instincts. I usually have a gut instinct, but then I will survey people that I trust in our companies and people on my own team. I’m learning to be a better listener. When I hear people, as soon as in my mind, I feel like I know what they’re saying, I tend to then jump ahead to the next... I’m deposing them. I have a million questions.
I’m learning to be a better listener and kind of understand where they’re coming from. Then I take all of it, and I synthesize it. And I would say about maybe 60 percent of the time I end up with my original gut reaction, but 40 percent of the time I take a different path because of what I’ve heard and the expertise of those who are around me. So it takes a little longer than it maybe should, and you don’t always have time. Sometimes you have to make a snap decision, but on something really big, like what strategy are we going to take? I live in this world of creator rights where I’m thinking in one direction, but what would you argue on the other side? How are you looking at this?” And when that informs your decision-making, not only are you more prepared, but sometimes you will alter the way you think about something by putting yourself in their shoes and understanding there’s another side to this that’s going to make sense to a judge or to a policymaker because they’re not crazy. They have a different take, and it’s pretty valid.
Sometimes I have to be a moderating force even in my own industry, saying, “We’re living in our bubble, they’re living in their bubble, and so if we’re going to be effective at finding a solution, if that’s what we want, then we may have to think about this in a way that leads to a landing zone.” If we don’t want a solution and what we’re trying to do is make good trouble, that’s okay. A longstanding trope at The Verge started by our former colleague, Sarah Jeong, is that copyright law is the only functional law on the internet. The only way you actually really want to regulate the internet is to take things down. That is the thing that people want to accomplish. The First Amendment basically prohibits the government from creating some mechanism to take things down, except in the case of copyright law, where we have the Digital Millennium Copyright Act.
