Great. So this is why it took three years, and it’s still going on, because what you’re saying is, first of all, you need to learn from the experience with the DMCA. It is the precedent we have, and there are obviously problems on both sides. You need to learn from those. The second is you need to create a new intellectual property right, in this case, much closer to trademark than to copyright, but still an intellectual property right, because that is, as you said, sort of the functional way of balancing that against the First Amendment. If you have an intellectual property right, you are allowed to remove it despite somebody’s other free speech rights. In this case, there’s a weird analysis of, do you have a free speech right to control how your voice is used? So it’s like free speech versus free speech.
What we did was, besides getting together with many First Amendment law scholars and trying to hammer this out, which was a fascinating learning process, by the way... I feel like I got to go back to law school and listen to these brilliant constitutional scholars talk about the tension between the First Amendment and intellectual property rights. What you have to do, if you’re going to create a takedown regime, is put in hurdles on both sides. You have to put in hurdles on the “I’m telling you to take it down” side. And there are lots of things we’ve learned from the past, like: Are we going to force a, in this case, First Amendment review before you can send the notice? What’s the punishment if you send a false notice? Is that punishment high enough to deter false notices? Then on the back end, you have to have a counter notice, right? And then how do you make sure that that works well and that it’s not too low a hurdle, but a little bit of a hurdle because you want to have balance on both sides?
And then finally you have this middle area where there’s going to be a decision about whether or not it’s a parody, for example, which many are, and the First Amendment trumps copyright when it comes to a parody. What if it’s news? And what is news anymore? What is bona fide news versus some of the stuff I’m getting when I’m scrolling? We then created this middle period where a temporary restraining order, a very quick legal action, could take place and a judge could actually decide the constitutional question — because nobody wants the platforms deciding constitutional questions. The people on both sides are like regular people. They’re not going to be making ultimate determinations. So that’s ultimately what we came down to in the NO FAKES Act, which is the name of the federal bill that’s now being pushed. And whether the balance there is perfect or not yet, I don’t know, but I do know that we learned a lot of lessons from the DMCA.
I think everybody is very aware that the First Amendment defenses are really paramount in any kind of regime like this, and that overprotecting on either side… If you overprotect on the First Amendment side, then this also applies to a girl who’s bullied in high school and some kid takes her face and sticks it on a body that’s not hers. You don’t want that staying up when it shouldn’t. On the other hand, I have the right to use your face for certain things because that’s my free speech, and it’s really funny, or I’m making a point about underlying character or something like that. We ultimately got to a place where I don’t think folks are thrilled on all sides of it, but I think they think it’s progress.

What’s so fascinating to me about YouTube is that it is the first real lesson in the arc of the DMCA. It’s where I think a technology-based company realized that even if you win the fight on intellectual property rights, if you don’t have a partnership through a license in the actual market where fans are, you are not going to have the service that fans really want. And so it was the first time that everybody realized that you can win the case but lose the business. Music is such a driver of YouTube, and I think this applies to AI too. If what you’re creating substitutes for something else, it’s probably not fair use. That’s what we’re arguing in our case against Suno. You’re basically creating music that is competing on the same platform right next to human-made music; you can click on either one, and you’re paying the same subscription fee. And so you’re affecting the economic pool, and you’re effectively substituting in the marketplace.
This is the fourth factor of the fair use regime.
This is the fourth factor of fair use, which courts say is the most important: are you affecting the potential market for the underlying work? And if you are, that’s sort of problem number one. And already, Deezer’s going in one direction, Apple’s going in another direction, Spotify’s going in another direction. To me, the fully generated problem, which is a DIY problem, is a distributor problem. And we have to provide incentives to the distributors to get them to take responsibility and play ball.
Do you think that technology exists to support the policy there? You need a technology that can detect AI-generated media. I’m not sure that any of that exists or works well.
I think it exists and works well for fully generated AI music. We also do a lot of testing at the RIAA. That’s another thing that our tech team does. And then we disclose the results back to the folks who gave it to us. We won’t disclose it to anybody else, but if you want to know what our test says about your technology, we’ll tell you.
And I think when it comes to fully generated AI, there’s plenty of detection technologies out there that do a really good job. Once you get below that, time will make it better. So I don’t know that we could get into a lot of gradations right now. Deezer, very successfully, on a platform level, uses AI detection technology and then labels what it detects as fully generated AI, and it’s got a very low false positive rate.
I want to end by talking about the certifications for platinum records and so on. It’s an important part of what you do. All the artists want their little records on their wall. It’s amazing that it’s still records. One of our jokes at The Verge is also that no one knows how to count anything, that Nielsen ratings — I should probably disclose, we are now part of the company that owns Luminate, which powers the Billboard charts.
The Billboard charts and their methodology are always in flux. Actually, I think as of this year, they’re in a fight with YouTube. YouTube does not want to be counted on the Billboard charts because some methodologies are... Counting is very political.
It is.
You literally give awards for counting to a big number. That is in flux as artists gain more attention on TikTok. And I have probably heard that whole Nicole Kidman song, in fragments on TikTok. I’ve never listened to the whole thing all the way through, and I’m certainly never going to buy a copy of it. Again, all in flux, and then somewhere in there is a bunch of AI remixes, and now I’ve listened to “Pop Star” by Drake 10,000 times because Darth Vader is singing it to me.
How are you thinking about that methodology, as to who’s creating what? AI is in the mix, and we’re listening to more and more fragments to discover songs on social platforms than anything else.
I swear to God, you are in my daily meetings.
Can I just tell you? I’m happy to hear that. I drive The Verge team crazy because I’m like, the music industry is the future always. And they’re like, no one wants to listen to that. So thank you for indulging me. I appreciate you.
I mean, you have your finger on the pulse. This is exactly the type of stuff we’re thinking of. So right now we’re still in the world of 1500 streams equaling one unit, and what used to be the sale of a CD. Now it’s obviously singles-based more than albums-based, although we still do certify albums. And if you look at the chart eligibility program that is now being implemented outside of Billboard and OCC, in other places of the world, they have made rules to say, unless it’s substantially human, we are not going to allow it to be eligible for the chart because you’re literally taking the place of a human artist on number 49. Billboard, so far, will allow it, but they’ll label it.
We haven’t, because we certify albums that were released by record companies. We have yet to run into the issue of the AI slop or the machine-created piece. But as we get more into assistive AI, as creators start to use AI more, and you look at the chart eligibility of substantially human, does a stream as part of that 1500 mean that it still has to be a human stream? Yes, I’m sure that we will come down on that side.
But what does substantially human mean? I think over time that might change. It might be different three years from now than it is today. But at the core, it’s got to be in the control of the creator. And some people would argue that putting nine words into a music generator is an act of creation.
Oh, they will. They’re going to. Yeah.
And that they are a creator, and therefore it’s the same thing. It’s not the same thing. Not saying that craft doesn’t change over time, and that in songwriting it’s also different than in producing and creating a recording. Using AI in the songwriting process may look very different than it does in the recording process, so we have to think about that too. But as far as gold and platinum go, we are still in the reliably safe zone of being able to know with a great deal of certainty exactly what we’re doing. I think the evolution over time is going to be in how creators use AI more than it will need to be in something that’s fully machine-readable or machine-created.
Well, Mitch, you’ve given us so much time. As you can tell, I’ve thoroughly enjoyed this conversation. I could keep going for hours and hours now.
Me too. I mean, honestly, this has been awesome. You freaked me out a little bit because you... It’s so great to see, though, because the stuff that you’re focused on is exactly what we are trying to grapple with every single day. And I think where we’ve come to is that we can’t pretend that there are easy answers. We can’t just react sort of in a knee-jerk way. We’ve got to try to figure out a path forward that’s going to allow the industry to change and grow. This industry’s adapted more times than any other industry in the history of our country. I mean, nobody goes from wax cylinders to AI in a hundred years. Can you imagine asking Boeing to make cars? So, a very adaptable industry.
I agree with you that we’re ahead of the game and that we are the future. We’re sort of living it. And the lessons that we learned from the music industry, we can apply to a lot of other things. So this has been awesome.
Thank you so much for being on Decoder. Really appreciate it.
You got it. Take care.

Here’s when the Black Friday sales start at Walmart, Target, and other retailers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-09
15:07:23 UTC
00:07:23 KST

Black Friday officially kicks off on November 27th, but if you plan to make that the only day you buy gifts this holiday season, you’re missing out. Several prominent retailers, including Best Buy and Walmart, are preparing to roll out their holiday discounts both in-store and online. Best Buy is even offering price protection through the holiday shopping season on select goods, so if you buy early and the same item drops in price, you can get the better deal retroactively.
Here’s when the Black Friday sales start at Walmart, Target, and other retailers
Black Friday is just around the corner, and the early sales are about to begin.
That being said, it’s important to know how every major retailer is handling the shopping event this year, whether you plan to take advantage of the slew of early holiday deals or hold off until the day after Thanksgiving. If you plan to spend some cash, here are the schedules and expectations for Amazon, Walmart, Best Buy, and all the major retailers we know of.
Amazon has yet to announce its full Black Friday playbook, but the online retailer has dropped a few early deals in its so-called Holiday Shop, including steep discounts on Sony’s WH-1000XM6 headphones, the Google Pixel 11 Pro XL, and fitness trackers like the Fitbit Inspire 3. Just be aware that Amazon does not offer price matching, so price “protection” for many Amazon shoppers means buying the item at the lower price point and returning the original — which, unfortunately, is pretty wasteful.
Like in previous years, Walmart plans to roll out its Black Friday deals in three distinct waves. The first runs from November 12th through November 15th, starting online at 12:01AM ET and in stores at 6AM local time. Walmart Plus members will also get early access to some deals beginning at 12:01AM ET on November 12th, with the sale opening up to everyone at 12:01AM ET on November 13th.
Walmart’s official Black Friday sale then kicks off at 12:01AM on Monday, November 23rd, with Walmart Plus members once again getting early access to select deals online. Whatever “hot Deal drops” remain will then be available to non-members at 12:01AM ET on November 24th.
Walmart’s in-store Black Friday sale will then kick off at 6AM local time on November 27th. The retailer’s Cyber Monday sale, meanwhile, will kick off online at 12:01AM ET on November 30th and run through December 2nd.
The retailer hasn’t shared many deal specifics yet, but did offer a sneak peek in a recent press release promising discounts across a range of categories, including toys, fashion, beauty, and home goods.
Best Buy officially kicked off its Black Friday promos on October 30th, with the retailer launching its first set of doorbuster deals on Halloween. Like last year, Best Buy will drop subsequent deals every Friday in the run-up to the holidays, and those who sign up for My Best Buy Plus or My Best Buy Total will also get up to $25 in bonus rewards during select doorbuster events.
As for Best Buy’s main Black Friday event, the promos are slated to begin on November 19th and run for 10 days. The retailer will then hold its Cyber Sunday and Cyber Monday sale, followed by another round of Cyber Week deals, which will run from December 1st through the 6th. Best Buy also plans to hold a Last-Minute Savings event from December 18th through the 24th, giving shoppers yet another opportunity to save on holiday gifts.
Additionally, Best Buy shoppers get holiday price protection, which means that if you purchase a qualifying item and its price drops at Best Buy during the eligible holiday period, you can request a refund for the difference. The retailer is also extending its holiday return window, allowing most purchases made between October 30th and December 31st to be returned through January 15th, 2027, or January 31st for My Best Buy Plus and Total members.
Target’s early Black Friday sale ran from November 5th through November 7th, but the retailer also announced that it will introduce new limited-time deals every weekend throughout the holiday season. In addition, Target has brought back its “Deal of the Day” promotion, offering a new deal every day from November 1st through December 24th, with a one-day preview of upcoming offers.
GameStop has yet to announce its full Black Friday 2026 sale lineup, including specific discounts on games, consoles, and accessories. In prior years, the retailer has opened as early as 7AM local time on Black Friday, though the exact hours may vary by location. We’ll update this post as more details become available.
Newegg is kicking off the holiday shopping season with its Black November event, offering a new round of doorbuster deals every day from November 1st through November 30th. New discounts drop daily at 12PM ET, with deals available in limited quantities while supplies last. Shoppers can also preview the following day’s offers starting at 12PM ET.
Costco has already kicked off its Black Friday sale, with deals rolling out in two waves: October 30th through November 15th and November 16th through the 30th. The wholesale retailer will also offer online deals on Thanksgiving Day (Costco stores will be closed on the holiday itself), followed by a larger Black Friday sale, which runs from November 27th through the 30th. A separate, online-only Cyber Monday event will take place on November 30th.
Update, November 9th: Added new details for Walmart, Best Buy, and other retailers for the 2026 shopping season.

On Being an Engineer in 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-09
15:07:23 UTC
00:07:23 KST

Are We Still Needed?
We all feel it. Every other week, we lose or delegate another part of our work to agents. It started with giving up on writing code. Then it expanded to pretty much any writing - Slack messages, documents, emails. Since around Opus 4.6, debugging, once an art and something that made us proud, became clicking on the recommended option in Cursor. And with better harnesses, even architecture and high-level thinking started moving to agents.
My day-to-day now mostly consists of making sure my agents aren't blocking other people's agents (which is another topic worth writing about).
This naturally leads us to think that this is it. We, engineers, are doomed.
But before you start thinking, again, about which jobs are "AI-protected", let's take a step back.
We still have some real leverage over agents, and let me try to prove it using my favorite mathematical trick - reductio ad absurdum, aka "proof by contradiction".
- Assume we have no real leverage over agents. The agents are doing all the thinking, and we're just getting in their way.
- We all have access to roughly the same models and harnesses.
- So, if the human doesn't matter, the difference between engineers' output should shrink dramatically.
- But that's not what we're seeing. Great engineers are still producing much better results than average engineers. If anything, 10x engineers have become 100x engineers. And the average engineer is still average.
- Therefore, there's still something the human brings to the table.
But there's a problem with proof by contradiction - it shows if an assumption is wrong, but it doesn't tell you why.
So What Is It?
Now that we've established that humans still have some leverage, let's try to understand what it actually is.
Let's reverse-engineer it from a few observations:
- (Sometimes) agents get lost when the problem isn't defined well enough. I tend to keep asking questions until I feel we're solving the actual problem.
- (Sometimes) agents overcomplicate simple things or oversimplify complex ones. I have some intuition about which problems are hard and which ones can be kept simple.
- (Sometimes) agents can solve a problem without having to live with the solution. I have to think about whether it'll still make sense two years from now.
- Some things I can't put my finger on. I know something is wrong, but can't really explain why (what we call "intuition").
A cool example of that last point is our allergy to AI slop. We all know that feeling when we read less than a single sentence and immediately *know* that an AI wrote it, so we just stop reading. We don't necessarily know why, but something feels off.
We've even developed a whole language around it - slop, slop canon, slop grande, and an entire meme culture. We've developed a collective taste for what feels like slop without ever explicitly defining what that means.
Anyway, going back to the observations list - you could argue, of course, that all of this is temporary. With Opus n+1, we're done.
That might be true. But I've been hearing this for three years now, and somehow we are still here. So maybe in order to predict when we'll become obsolete we need to understand why we haven't become obsolete yet.
And for that, let's use one of the oldest questions in philosophy.
On Human Consciousness
For centuries, philosophers have tried to answer a seemingly simple question - what is consciousness? What makes us, us?
We've studied the brain, its cells, neurons, even our DNA. Yet we still can't fully explain how consciousness emerges from all these individual parts.
While reading about this topic, I came across two concepts that clicked for me. Together, they seemed to explain what I was looking for:
- Emergence - the idea that something can arise from the interactions of many smaller parts, even though none of those parts has that property on its own.
- Tacit Knowledge - an idea by the philosopher Michael Polanyi that "we can know more than we can tell" - things we know but can't easily explain.
I'm not suggesting that consciousness explains why we're better at some things than agents (or even that agents won't have consciousness), but it made me think about how much of who we are comes from things we can't easily describe.
Much of that comes from experience. A random conversation, something that happened years ago, a thought during a morning run. None of them matters much on its own, but together they shape who we are.
We Will (Probably) Still Be Needed
Models already outsmart us in many ways. They have agency and they're developing taste - at least the kind of taste you can learn from reading everything we've ever written. Both will keep improving. Maybe Opus n+1 will close the gap even further.
But I think there's a difference between knowing everything about something and actually experiencing it.
We're still the ones having random conversations, making mistakes, developing opinions, having fears and desires. All those things shape who we are, and in turn, how we approach problems and what we build.
I keep asking questions because I've built a solution to the wrong problem before. I have a feeling about what problems are genuinely hard because I've been outsmarted by the ones that looked easy. I care about the next two years because I solved problems two years ago and I learned what works and what doesn't. And that thing I can't put my finger on - the thing that makes us allergic to slop - is an experience I never consciously stored.
Even caring about not blocking other people's agents is, ten layers down, about being afraid of getting fired and wanting to be excellent at what I do - 2026's mix of impostor syndrome and pride in the craft.
Maybe one day agents will have their own experiences, too. Maybe they'll develop intuitions they can't quite explain, just like we do.
But until then, our leverage isn't just in what we know, but in everything we've experienced that made us who we are.

Here are the shipping and return policies for all the big-name retailers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-09
15:07:13 UTC
00:07:13 KST

With the holidays quickly approaching, everyone will soon be on the hunt for gifts and the fastest way to get them. Thankfully, many retailers offer generous shipping policies, with some even providing free two-day shipping or same-day delivery if you’re willing to pay a little extra. And just in case the gift you choose isn’t quite right, many retailers offer extended return policies so your giftee can get something more to their liking.
Here are the shipping and return policies for all the big-name retailers
We’ve read the fine print and rounded up the policies for each major retailer to make things simpler.
For your convenience, we’ve compiled the current shipping and return policies for all the big-name retailers, from Amazon to Walmart. A few already have holiday policies in place, but we’ll be keeping tabs on them and updating our list accordingly. Hopefully, knowing more about how much leeway you have to make a return will help lessen that inevitable holiday angst (fingers crossed).
Amazon
Shipping: Same-day delivery is not available on Thanksgiving, Christmas, or New Year’s (it’s also limited on Black Friday). However, Prime members get free same-day delivery on qualifying orders in qualifying ZIP codes provided they meet the “minimum qualifying dollar threshold” (which varies by location) of eligible items in their cart. One-Day and Two-Day Delivery with no minimum purchase amount required is also available to Prime members for qualifying products. Non-Prime buyers will find shipping options on the order page of each specific product.
Returns: As part of its holiday promotional period, Amazon says most items purchased between November 1st and December 31st can be returned until January 31st, 2027. Apple products, however, must be returned by January 15th, 2027. Note that this policy applies to both Prime and non-Prime buyers.
Apple
Shipping: Apple has yet to provide details on its holiday shipping policy; however, last year, it offered free delivery of in-stock items that hadn’t been engraved by Christmas Eve if you ordered before 9PM ET on December 21st. Apple also offers free next-day or two-hour delivery from local stores in most metro areas for an additional fee, or you can opt to pick up purchases yourself by visiting your local Apple Store.
Returns: Apple is offering an extended return period for online orders received between November 6th and December 25th, allowing you to return items until January 8th, 2027. Purchases made after December 25th are generally subject to the usual terms and conditions, and must be returned within 14 calendar days of your initial purchase date.
Target
Shipping: Target offers free two-day shipping on many orders if you spend $35 or more or use your Target Circle Card. Same-day delivery costs $9.99 per order, but it’s included with a Target Circle 360 membership ($10.99 a month / $99 a year). Your mileage may vary for same-day delivery availability based on the item and your location.
Returns: Target offers an extended return policy for electronics and entertainment items purchased between November 1st and December 24th, allowing you to return them until January 24th, 2027. Mobile phones and Apple products (including Beats products) purchased during the same window must be returned by January 8th, 2027. Target’s standard return policy applies for most other items, with a generous 90-day window for third-party products and up to a year for Target-branded products with a receipt.
Walmart
Shipping: Walmart’s holiday shipping policy doesn’t currently mention a deadline for delivery by Christmas, but it does break down the available fulfillment options. Walmart provides free next-day delivery in eligible ZIP codes, free two-day delivery, and free standard shipping for eligible orders of $35 or more. Walmart Plus subscribers also receive free next-day and two-day shipping with no order minimum. Some orders and ZIP codes may also qualify for same-day delivery, if you’re willing to pay an additional fee.
Returns: Most items purchased between October 1st and December 31st may be returned until January 31st, 2027. Some exceptions, like smartphones, may apply.
B&H Photo
Shipping: B&H Photo offers free two-day and next-day shipping on select items. Most other products qualify for free standard shipping (one to seven business days), and free expedited shipping (one to two business days) is generally available for items over $49.
Returns: B&H Photo allows returns within 30 days of the delivery date, provided the items are in new condition and still housed in their original packaging. For the holidays, most items purchased between November 1st and January 1st can be returned until February 1st, 2027.
Best Buy
Shipping: Best Buy is offering free next-day and two-day shipping on qualifying orders for My Best Buy Plus and My Best Buy Total members. Non-members, meanwhile, can get free next-day shipping on qualifying orders totaling $35 or more. Same-day delivery is also available on select items, seven days a week, and you can check your eligibility by entering your ZIP code in Best Buy’s online portal.
Returns: Best Buy offers a 15-day return window for most products, while “activatable” items like smartphones and wearables, which come with a third-party contract, must be returned within 14 days. My Best Buy Plus and My Best Buy Total members have up to 60 days to make returns, though the 14-day limit still applies to activatable products.
For the holidays, Best Buy has an extended return window, which allows most products purchased between October 30th and December 31st to be returned until January 15th, 2027. The exceptions above surrounding activatable devices still apply, and holiday decorations are also limited to 15 days regardless of their purchase date.
Costco
Shipping: At Costco, shipping fees vary by product and shipping method, although shipping is often free. The wholesale retailer also offers a variety of delivery options, including “white glove” service for larger appliances. Same-day delivery is also available on some items via Costco’s partnership with Instacart.
Returns: Costco generally has an open return policy, except for electronics such as TVs and computers, which have a 90-day return window. Other exceptions are listed on its return page.
GameStop
Shipping: GameStop currently offers free shipping only to GameStop Pro members on orders of $54 or more. It also offers same-day delivery in certain locations if you order from your local store at least three hours before the store closes.
Returns: GameStop hasn’t listed its holiday return policy yet, but you can return products within 15 days, provided the packages are unopened and you have the receipt. Pro members, meanwhile, get 30 days.
Dell
Shipping: Most Dell products include free standard shipping (no minimum purchase required). The delivery window can vary based on your order, but Dell also offers expedited and express shipping options, along with a delivery date estimate based on the ZIP code you provide at checkout. Orders placed by December 23rd with qualifying express delivery windows are expected to arrive before December 25th; Dell’s 2026 Holiday Shipping and Delivery Schedule outlines additional shipping times based on which speed you choose.
Returns: Under Dell’s extended return policy, you can return purchases made between November 1st and December 29th until January 15th, 2027.
DJI
Shipping: DJI offers free shipping on purchases of $200 or more. Otherwise, shipping fees are specified on the order form. Shipment times can vary for each product depending on availability.
Returns: DJI offers returns within 14 days of receiving the purchase, provided the item remains in like-new condition or suffers from a manufacturing defect.
Shipping: All standard orders qualify for free shipping with no minimum. Just note that this applies to the lowest-cost shipping available, which may not be the fastest.
Returns: Google hasn’t announced any special holiday return policies yet. For now, all purchases are covered by the standard terms and conditions, which let you return most items within 15 days of receiving them. Nest Thermostats and Verizon contract phones, however, come with an extended 30-day return window.
HP
Shipping: For many items, standard shipping is free and arrives within three to six days. HP also offers expedited and priority shipping options for an additional fee. The company will not ship or deliver items on Christmas, Thanksgiving, or New Year’s Day.
Returns: You can return most items purchased from HP’s website within 30 days of delivery. There are exceptions, though, and select items may be subject to a restocking fee of up to 15 percent.
Microsoft
Shipping: Most products sold through the online Microsoft Store include free two- or three-day shipping, with express shipping available for an additional fee.
Returns: You can return most physical products purchased online for free through January 31, 2027, as long as they’re in like-new condition. The item must be in its original packaging, with all parts, manuals, and other accessories included. Items exempt from this policy include digital gift cards, gift cards for services and subscriptions, and select hardware, such as the ROG Xbox Ally and Ally X, Surface for Business devices, and HoloLens.
Newegg
Shipping: Many of Newegg’s items come with free shipping and are delivered within one to five business days; for details, check the individual product page.
Returns: Qualifying items purchased between November 1st and December 31st can be returned or replaced until January 31st, 2027.
Sam’s Club
Shipping: According to the Sam’s Club FAQ, shipping costs for most items vary based on the item’s size, weight, shipping method, and delivery address. Plus Members get free shipping on many online items, and same-day delivery or curbside pickup is available for free if you’re a Plus member ($120 a year) and place a qualifying order totaling $50 or more by 1PM local time. Club members ($60 a year) can pay $12 for same-day or next-day shipping, or get free curbside pickup.
Returns: Sam’s Club does not have a specified return period; however, some products may have specific return periods stated. For example, electronics and major appliances have a 90-day return window, while phones are subject to a 14-day return policy.
Sonos
Shipping: Sonos offers free shipping on all products, with in-stock items typically shipping the same day if purchased by 11AM local time. You can also pay extra for two-day or express shipping.
Returns: Sonos offers a 30-day return policy and even provides free return shipping. However, you must have bought the product directly from Sonos, and you must initiate the return within 30 days of receiving your purchase. The product must also include the original packaging and be in new or as-new condition to be eligible.
Update, November 9th: Updated to reflect shipping deadlines and return policies for the 2026 holiday season.

How to shop like a pro during Black Friday and Cyber Monday
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-09
15:07:00 UTC
00:07:00 KST

Despite Amazon and other retailers filling the summer and fall months with more sales than ever before, Black Friday and Cyber Monday remain the biggest shopping days of the year. And, in recent years, the sale periods have started earlier, giving you more time to take advantage of the deals.
How to shop like a pro during Black Friday and Cyber Monday
The annual deal extravaganza can be overwhelming, but the right tool and a little patience can help you score big.
We’re already hard at work to find the best prices on phones, accessories, 4K TVs, noise-canceling headphones, gaming gear, and other tech throughout the deal-packed weeks culminating in the big events, whether you plan to shop in person or online.
You can always count on us to publish only the best deals that you need to know about, no matter the season. However, if you want to be among the first people to spot price drops on the products you’re interested in, you’ll want to get a head start on your Black Friday and Cyber Monday game plan. Thankfully, we have a few suggestions for scouting early sales at your favorite retailers, finding the right price-tracking tool, and setting up email alerts to ensure you don’t miss rare discounts at Amazon and elsewhere.
Leverage a price-tracking tool or deal aggregator
The most effective way to find a truly great deal is to set up a price-tracking tool. We’ve included a few of our favorites below, many of which we use daily here at The Verge. Each can help you track deals at various retailers — including Amazon, Walmart, Best Buy, and Target — but they each do so differently and come with their own set of advantages / disadvantages.
All of them are free to use, and once you’ve added the products you’re interested in keeping an eye on, you can rest easy knowing that you don’t need to take any action until it comes time to make a purchase. Just make sure you keep your email notifications on so you see the alerts as they come in.
CamelCamelCamel is arguably the most popular price-tracking tool at The Verge, and for good reason: it’s incredibly useful since it tracks the price of every product sold on Amazon and can send you alerts when an item falls to a customizable price threshold. Once a product reaches the desired price you’ve set (or lower), you’ll get an email about it. You can use the extension’s price graph to determine what price is likely to happen based on historical data, but it’s always a shot in the dark.
To track prices and get alerts via email, you’ll need to create a free CamelCamelCamel account. Additionally, we suggest installing the site’s browser extension, The Camelizer, which works with Google Chrome, Safari, Mozilla Firefox, Opera, and Microsoft Edge. The handy tool lets you view pricing trends on a product-by-product basis and set your desired price without leaving Amazon. It’s fantastic, easy to use, and works in several countries, including the US, UK, Canada, Germany, Spain, France, Italy, and Australia.
As mentioned, the tracker only works for products listed on Amazon. However, in May, the company released CamelMart, its price tracker for Walmart. While it doesn’t have a browser extension (yet), its functionality is similar to CamelCamelCamel in that you can set price alerts and email notifications, so you’ll always know when your desired price threshold for a particular product is met.
Like CamelCamelCamel, Keepa is another handy tool for tracking product prices on Amazon. Keepa has charts that track pricing trends and can alert you when it finds a deal. Similarly, you can also import any of your Amazon wishlists.
Unlike CamelCamelCamel, however, you don’t necessarily need to create an account to track prices with Keepa; just install the appropriate browser extension for Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Firefox, or Opera, and Keepa will automatically add a price history graph to supported product listings. The embedded graph shows pricing history and allows you to specify various pricing details. If you set a desired price, Keepa will send you a price alert via email, push notification, Telegram, or RSS.
Slickdeals aggregates some of the best deals around the internet, as discovered by its team and community of users. Its site also lets you browse coupons and create deal alerts based on specific keywords, though the latter works a little differently on Slickdeals than it does with the sites above.
You can type in a product name, like “Nintendo Switch 2,” “OLED TVs,” or a retailer’s name, and once it’s added to your list, you’ll get a deal alert if it meets your criteria. You can set it to alert you to literally any deal related to your keyword, or you can filter out deals so you’ll only be notified if, for example, the deal is popular enough to make it to Slickdeals’ front page or earns a high rating from the community. If you like browsing deals, it’s generally a good idea to visit Slickdeals frequently, especially since it usually has a Black Friday component that allows you to browse circulars for Best Buy, Target, and other retailers in advance.
Also, it’s just fun to see what the community digs up.
For a more hands-off way to see whether you’re getting a good deal, try your browser’s built-in tools. For a few years now, Edge has been able to tell you when you’re looking at the best price for a particular product from a range of retailers, and Google Chrome can track price fluctuations and notify you when a particular product goes on sale. Edge and Chrome are available on Windows, macOS, and Linux, as well as Android and iOS.
Use Alexa for Shopping, Amazon’s capable AI chatbot
You may have already noticed that sometimes, when you’re shopping on Amazon, a sidebar opens to reveal more information about the product you’re looking at. Even if you haven’t used it, you can’t miss it; it’s prominently featured in Amazon’s upper nav bar and accessible by clicking the Price History button on a given listing.
Whether you’re using the Amazon app or the website, it’s a capable tool that, at its core, does some of the same tasks as our other recommendations. It can send price alerts and show up to a year’s worth of pricing data, helping you make informed buying decisions for products on Amazon. It can also recommend alternatives that might be a better value and, if you’ll allow it, can even automatically purchase products on your behalf.
It can do a lot more, too. For instance, you can have it update you when, say, a specific product launches, and it can shop on your behalf by adding specified items to your cart at a specified frequency. You can also use it to compare products sold on Amazon, and even upload photos of wishlists to find matching products.
Set up deal alerts for Alexa or the Amazon app
If you have an Alexa-compatible smart gadget, such as an older Echo Dot Max or one of the company’s newer Echo devices, you can ask the virtual assistant to alert you when specific products go on sale. You can receive alerts up to 24 hours in advance of planned price drops for eligible products, or as soon as it notices a discount on anything saved in your shopping cart or wish list. If you say, “Alexa, buy it for me,” after being notified of the deal, the assistant will purchase the item for you once the discount becomes available.
To enable these features, open the Alexa app on your smartphone and navigate to More > Settings > Notifications > Amazon Shopping. Then, toggle the slider next to Deal Recommendations within the Shopping Recommendations section. Alexa will audibly notify you of deals moving forward, but if you happen to miss one, you can check for the notification on your phone or see whether you have any new notifications on an Echo device by checking for the yellow light. If it’s lit, just say, “Alexa, play notifications.”
You can receive similar notifications on your smartphone from the Amazon Shopping app, too. Just open the app and go to Settings > Notifications > Deals and recommendations, and toggle the slider next to the Savings option.
Check retailer schedules and plan for early shopping events
Keeping an eye on preferred retailers before Black Friday will help save you time (and money). Several major retailers have already detailed their plans in the run-up to the holidays, and many will offer early opportunities to save. For example:
- Walmart is hosting three online shopping events for Black Friday and Cyber Monday. Its first event runs from November 12th through the 15th, serving as a preview of sorts. The second runs from November 23rd to the 29th, encapsulating Black Friday and the days surrounding it. Finally, it switches to Cyber Monday on November 30th, with deals lasting through December 2nd. Walmart Plus customers get a 24-hour lead on deals, as in previous years, and any remaining deals will open to all customers afterward. In-store events are also scheduled for November 12th through the 15th, as well as November 27th (Black Friday), each starting at 6AM local time. Walmart’s Cyber Monday deals are online-only and start at 12:01AM ET.
- Target is going all in on early shopping this year, with a three-day shopping event happening from November 5th through the 7th, with new limited-time offers every weekend. The retailer will also host a new “Deal of the Day” each day through December 24th.
- Best Buy kicked off its early Black Friday event on Friday, October 30th. That’s done, but it’s continuing with deal events throughout the year. New doorbuster deals will drop every Friday, and its first early Black Friday event starts on November 6th. The retailer’s extended Black Friday sale will begin immediately afterward on November 19th and run through the 28th, offering a chance to save on previous doorbusters and some Black Friday exclusives. It’ll then transition into a two-day Cyber Monday sale, which will take place on November 29th and November 30th. Finally, it’ll host a “last-minute savings event” between December 18th and the 24th.
You can expect more major retailers to detail their Black Friday plans shortly, so keep an eye on their respective websites and start filling your calendar accordingly.
Pay close attention to lightning deals and doorbusters
Doorbusters, lightning deals, and other limited-time discounts are a tried-and-true hallmark of any Black Friday sale. They’ll usually be the most buzzworthy deals you’ll see all year, with truly low prices to spark impulsive spending. As you’re checking ads, make a note of these deals and read all of the fine print surrounding their availability. Some may require you to sign up in advance or get in line early (ahem, Amazon), and some can be so scarce that you won’t have the entire weekend — or even an hour — to claim them.
Have a price-matching backup plan
Although many stores will automatically match their competitors’ pricing, sometimes you may need to twist their arm. It’s helpful to know the various price-matching policies of each retailer in the event that your preferred store runs out of stock on certain goods. You can get up to speed with our price-matching guide, which details the lengths each retailer will or won’t go to win your dollar. Unfortunately, some retailers put a temporary halt on their usual policies during special shopping events like Black Friday, but it never hurts to ask.
Trust the experts
We’re a discerning bunch here at The Verge, so don’t fret if you’re going into Black Friday and Cyber Monday without any prep. We’ll be corralling the best tech deals and keeping our coverage up to date with new sale items while dropping old ones to avoid disappointment. While we usually suggest paying attention to deals starting the day after Thanksgiving — or November 27th, in this case — the truth is that several retailers typically jump the gun and start offering some great deals in the lead-up to the shopping holiday.
To catch every opportunity to save, be sure to bookmark our coverage, follow us on Bluesky, subscribe to our weekday Verge Deals newsletter, and start setting aside some cash for Black Friday and Cyber Monday.
Update 10:00AM ET, November 9th: We’ve added new ways to track prices for the upcoming 2026 holiday shopping season.

Medium is launching a new note-taking app called TK
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-09
15:05:42 UTC
00:05:42 KST

For the first time ever, Medium is becoming more than just a blogging platform. The company is launching a new app, called TK, that combines note taking and journaling with something resembling a private social network. The app is meant to get you writing more, and help you share that writing with friends and fans. And it’s part of a much bigger idea about blogging, and a much broader thesis about the state of the internet.
Medium is launching a new note-taking app called TK
The company is betting that the future of blogging looks a lot like group chats.
“I don’t think we’ve actually had a launch of anything important since 2017,” Medium CEO Tony Stubblebine tells me over Zoom, a few days ahead of the company’s biggest launch in apparently almost a decade. That was when Medium’s then-CEO, Ev Williams, decided to quit chasing ad dollars and become a subscription business. “It’s clear that the broken system is ad-driven media on the internet,” Williams wrote at the time. “It simply doesn’t serve people. In fact, it’s not designed to.” Medium began charging for access to most content. “We got out of the attention economy,” Stubblebine says now.
The trend Williams saw back then, though, has only accelerated and metastasized. AI companies are hoovering up any content they can get their hands on, legality be damned; search engines and chatbots are sending less and less traffic back to the web. Medium, like most websites on the internet, relies on Google for a huge portion of its traffic — in the time of Google Zero, that’s an existential risk. “When Google started taking away all the traffic,” Stubblebine says, “what I told them is that this hurts us, but it also hurts you, because I’ll just tell you what my product roadmap is going to do: I’m going to switch to private blogging… We’re just going to take everything underground.”
All of which brings us back to TK, an app and network that has no use or need for Google referrals. The idea behind TK is fairly straightforward: It’s a barebones note-taking app, with emphasis on daily journal-style notes and longer-form writing. The app itself is nice enough, like an ultra-minimalist take on Evernote, but it’s the stuff around the writing that has Stubblebine most excited.
For one thing, you can point an AI model at your writing, and use it to help organize or make sense of all the notes you’ve been taking, by searching through your notes or asking for feedback on your writing. “TK” is both the name of the app and a shortcut in it: type the letters (which writers use frequently as a placeholder — they’re easy to find later, since the letters T and K hardly ever appear next to each other otherwise) and you can summon the model to fill in a bit of information for you. Stubblebine refers to “Unix pipes” a few times in our conversation, and his idea is to use the large language models to do some of the grunt work of both creating and managing notes.
Once you’ve written something – and Stubblebine emphasizes that it doesn’t have to be a blog post — you can then share it however you like. You can share it via links or email the way you’d share a Google Doc, and collaborators can write, comment, and leave emoji reactions. You can also add your writing to what TK calls Libraries. Stubblebine calls the Libraries concept “private blogging,” which is a good metaphor. The early Libraries I’ve seen in the app are mostly centered around a topic, and people can contribute their writing on that topic. There’s no public face to any of it; it’s just a blog for and by its authors. Sometimes a few of them, sometimes a few hundred. There are groups sharing their ongoing book projects, swapping recipes, and posting poetry drafts, all for the eyes of only the other people in the group. It’s blogging meets group chats.
This concept of private blogging is a big part of the future of Medium. “Medium is, at some level, performative,” Stubblebine says. “You have to want to share yourself with the world.” But in a post-Google world, he says, that’s essentially impossible. TK doesn’t measure pageviews or reward authors for getting traffic. “This is a community that’s going to give you feedback and encouragement,” Stubblebine says. “It’s not about the drive to be noticed.” Features like this, he says, are coming to the broader Medium platform soon.
TK is now available, for free, via apps for the web, Android, and iOS. (Stubblebine says a native desktop app is also coming soon.) If TK works, though, it could be a crucial new way for Medium to make money. Obviously, Stubblebine says, there are ways to make money from private and paywalled content. That’s the newsletter business. But also, he wonders, what if there’s a way to package up all the best stuff from the Recipe Box library and charge people, or AI agents, for access? “The generic web is getting dumber and dumber,” Stubblebine says. If AI is the future, “it needs to be based on this layer of human intelligence.” And all that intelligence might be better off outside the confines of the Google algorithm.

I saw your HN comment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-09
15:01:03 UTC
00:01:03 KST

I Saw Your HN Comment
I used to love getting emails from people in response to things I’ve written online, blog posts or Hacker News comments, but in the last 2 years it’s changed from mostly signal to mostly noise. I’ve met people in real life as a result of these emails, I’ve hired people based on these emails, and I’ve learned cool things through these emails but today it’s almost all pitches. I (had Claude) look through all the emails I’ve gotten about my posts and comments since 2013 to check my gut feeling:
LLMs have made this much easier, they can write convincing emails personalized to a real comment I wrote on HN. What’s worse is that they are often very deceptive. They don’t come out and say they are pitching you something, they ask a question, posing as if they care about the answer. Something like:
Hi Josh, saw your HN comment about [thing you said]. [Compliment.] I’m curious, [open-ended question]?
If someone took the time to email me asking a question I almost always respond to it but I’m having to rethink that policy. It’s like having an amplification attack pointed at you, someone sends 2-3 sentences (sometimes more) with an open-ended question then I turn around and write 2-3+ paragraphs to answer the question, only to get a response that is pitching a product/service. Here are a few real pivots I’ve received:
- “That’s close to what I’m building…”
- “The tool I mentioned, [product], works from the other end…”
- “Worth saying this is what we build at [company], so I’m not a neutral party.”
- “Would you have 15 min next week?”
It saddens me that what was once a rare joy and way to meet interesting people is now being abused to send cold emails. Look, I get it, cold emails are a fact of life, I’ve sent them before as well, but the deceptive ones are where I draw the line. I would never waste someone’s time without being upfront about why I’m contacting them. Personally I find this “growth hacking” to be disgusting and I will never use a product advertised to me in this way.
Because these people are obscuring the real reason, it’s impossible to tell what is a real question and what is just a setup to pitch. I resent having to read every one of these emails as a potential pitch, but I also try not to assume the worst about everyone that reaches out. I wouldn’t want to snub someone because I thought they were going to pitch to me when they had a legitimate question or just wanted to talk. I’ve started sending short emails back and only if I don’t get a pitch back do I actually engage but I dislike feeling distrustful, treating people as guilty until proven innocent. I love talking about tech, I love talking to other people about cool things they are doing, I hate being advertised to and I hate it even more when it’s wrapped up in fake interest.
I know there is nothing HN can do about this, it’s not their fault, I publicly post my email address on my profile, that’s on me. In the past it’s led to serendipity, now it more often leads to frustration.
My comments used to introduce me to interesting people, now they’re mostly LLM context for a sales pitch, grist for the mill. The internet I pine for might not be coming back, but I can’t bring myself to take my email address down. I’ll keep separating the wheat from the chaff. But I’ll be grumpy about it.

Zebkit – Chromium's engine as a library you link, not a runtime you live in
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-09
14:34:00 UTC
23:34:00 KST

Chrome as a library — light, fast, everywhere, and easy.
One API on Linux, macOS and Windows. Add it in a few lines.
zebkit is Chromium's engine as one library you link into your own
application: Blink, V8 with every JIT tier, PDFium, FFmpeg and the rest of
what Chrome is made of, with nothing of Chrome's browser and nothing of
Electron's runtime. Your application stays yours, in C, C++, Rust, Python,
Go or JavaScript, with its own windows and toolkit. Where it needs the web,
it adds a zebkit view; where it needs a PDF, media, compression or crypto,
it calls zebkit's API: in C, or through the bindings for Rust, Python, Go
and JavaScript (zebkit-js, and zebkit.* in the application's own pages).
- Integrate it, don't build on it. Electron is a base: an application
is built inside it, on its runtime, its windows and its packaging.
zebkit is a part: an application adds it, as it adds SQLite, and keeps
its process, its toolkit and its way of shipping. It runs inside the
application's own event loop (zebkit_init(), zebkit_pump()), and draws
in the application's windows, as frames you draw or in a child of a window
you give it, an X11 window, an NSView or an HWND (examples/native-host),
and gives back the window a page is in for the system's dialogs.
- Take what you need. Web views, in a window or off-screen with their frames handed to you; a full PDF API; saving what a page plays; your own URL schemes; native UI from JavaScript; Playwright's API and CDP for agents. Use one, or all.
- The real Chrome engine. Pages see Chromium 157: its user agent and
client hints, window.chrome, popups blocked without a click, and
nothing of a debugger attached (docs/API.md has what still differs,
Google's sign-in among it).
- Lighter than Electron. Against the latest Electron, 45.2.1: 34% smaller, a cold start in 2.3 s against 6.6, a page in 29% less memory, and the DOM, text layout and JavaScript level (Benchmark).
- No Node. No second JavaScript runtime and no IPC through one. The
application is native code, or JavaScript run by zebkit-js on the
engine's V8.
- Chromium's libraries are yours. 17 C libraries inside the engine, about
7,490 functions on each of Linux, macOS and Windows (7,487 on all three, the
rest each system's own), exported under zebkit_vendor_*: SQLite, LevelDB, BoringSSL,
zlib, Zstandard, Brotli, ICU, HarfBuzz, libxml2, libwebp, libjpeg-turbo,
FFmpeg, dav1d, Opus, libvpx, FreeType and PDFium. You do not ship them twice.
- PDF built in. A full API on Chromium's PDFium: rendering and tiles, text with layout, search, outline, links, annotations as an editor has them (line endings, cloudy borders, free text with callouts and rich text, stamps, replies and states, measurement, XFDF and FDF), forms, redaction, page editing, merging, attachments, metadata, and signatures checked for integrity; hooks for an application's own annotation kinds, appearances, events with undo, render layers, OCR, fonts, trust and actions. In C, Rust, Python and JavaScript.
- 2D drawing and shaping. <zebkit/canvas.h> on the engine's Skia and <zebkit/text.h> on its HarfBuzz, without shipping either again.
- Media, saved as it plays. Whatever a page plays, a file, MSE/DASH or
HLS, written to MP4 or WebM as it was sent, without re-encoding and
without a second download (<zebkit/media.h>).
- Bytes as they are. A page's calls to the application go over its frame's own Mojo channel, large ones through shared memory: no base64, the page's JSON handed on as it was written, as fast as Electron's IPC for small calls and faster for large ones.
- The window around a page, from JavaScript. zebkit.ui draws
windows, prompts and dialogs with Chromium's views toolkit: signals,
JSX, Tailwind classes, and automation for tests and agents. Rich UI is
a page; zebkit.ui is the chrome around it (docs/UI.md).
- Playwright's API, natively. The whole of Playwright (locators,
actions that wait until they can be done, keyboard, mouse and touch,
routes, dialogs, downloads, contexts, workers, traces, HAR, video) runs
inside the engine, without CDP or a Node.js driver: 3 to 10 times faster
than Playwright over CDP, and a click in 3 to 5 ms instead of 33
(<zebkit/automation.h>, docs/AUTOMATION.md). Playwright's own
clients, in any of its languages, connect to it unchanged with chromium.connect().
- Made for agents. tools/zebkit-mcp gives them pages, PDFs, files, media
and native windows as MCP tools, over standard input and HTTP, within bounds
its operator sets (docs/MCP.md). They can also drive zebkit through
Playwright's API or over CDP, Chromium's own DevTools server, headless or
windowed.
- Customise it from your code, down to the desktop. Native hooks decide
what the engine does, in C, Rust, Python and JavaScript: permissions,
navigation, popups, dialogs, downloads, certificates and client
certificates, sign-in, network requests and responses at every stage,
settings at run time, your own URL schemes, what a page may call, scripts
before the page's own (docs/ROADMAP_HOOKS.md). And everything a page or
the engine would show the person or ask of the system goes through the
application: the window's frame (system, overlay or none, with the page as
the title bar), menus and the context menu, JavaScript dialogs and sign-in,
file and device choosers, screen capture, notifications, the tray, the
Dock and taskbar, sharing, the system's theme, power and displays
(Fit it into the desktop, docs/SYSTEM_INTEGRATION.md).
- Safe by default. A page has no zebkit object unless the
application grants it, per view, per origin and per capability; the
origin is the browser's, never the page's word; the renderer stays
sandboxed; permissions a browser would ask about are not granted.
A package is a directory with the library, the helper, the engine's data
and include/. Either unpack a release's archive
(zebkit-<version>-<target>.tar.xz from GitHub's releases), or build one:
mise run r      # dist/release (Linux), dist/release-macos (macOS), dist/release-windows; hours the first time
Each archive also holds the tools, built for its system beside the library
and ready to run from where it is unpacked: zebkit-run, zebkit-js and
zebkit-mcp (.exe on Windows, sandboxed there too).
On an Apple silicon Mac with full Xcode installed, scripts/dist.sh release
builds the engine locally into dist/release. Then run
scripts/example.sh macos-basic to build and launch the C embedding demo
in dist/example/Zebkit Embedded Browser.app.
Building needs about 30 GB for Chromium's tree (docs/BUILD.md). Below,
$PKG is the package directory.
zebkit is a library: your program keeps its main() and calls it. This
one renders a PDF's first page to a PNG and reads its text, with PDFium
and the image encoders inside zebkit, and nothing else to install:
#include <stdio.h>
#include <zebkit/pdf.h>
#include <zebkit/services.h>
/* Your program, your main(): zebkit is just a library it calls. */
int main(int argc, char **argv) {
    char *error = NULL;
    zebkit_pdf *pdf = zebkit_pdf_open_file(argv[1], NULL, &error);
    if (!pdf) {
        fprintf(stderr, "%s\n", error);
        return 1;
    }
    /* The first page as a PNG, at twice its size. */
    zebkit_pdf_render_options options = {.scale = 2, .background = 0xffffffff};
    int width, height;
    uint8_t *rgba = zebkit_pdf_render(pdf, 0, &options, &width, &height, &error);
    size_t size;
    uint8_t *png = zebkit_image_encode(ZEBKIT_IMAGE_PNG, rgba, width, height, 0, &size, &error);
    fwrite(png, 1, size, fopen("page1.png", "wb"));
    /* And its text. */
    char *text = zebkit_pdf_text(pdf, 0, &error);
    printf("%d pages; page 1 says: %.80s\n", zebkit_pdf_page_count(pdf), text);
    zebkit_free(text), zebkit_free(png), zebkit_free(rgba);
    zebkit_pdf_close(pdf);
    return 0;
}cc thumb.c -I$PKG/include -L$PKG -l:libzebkit.so.1 -Wl,-rpath,$PKG -o thumb   # Linux
cc thumb.c -I$PKG/include -F$PKG -framework Zebkit -Wl,-rpath,$PKG -o thumb   # macOS
./thumb report.pdf     # 2 pages; page 1 says: Quarterly report ...
The PDF API, compression, crypto, URLs, image codecs, ICU and the
libraries inside the engine (zebkit_vendor_*, FFmpeg's among them) need
no engine loop (docs/API.md); only HTTP through the engine's network
stack and web pages do.
Web pages need the engine running. Here the engine runs the loop: the
program starts it with zebkit_main() and works in its callbacks. A program
with its own loop (GTK, Qt, AppKit, winit) starts it with zebkit_init() and
calls zebkit_pump() (examples/native-host).
#include <stdio.h>
#include <zebkit/zebkit.h>
static void printed(zebkit_view *view, const char *json, const char *error, void *data) {
    printf("%s\n", json ? json : error);
    zebkit_quit();
}
static void loaded(zebkit_view *view, zebkit_load_event event, const char *url, void *data) {
    if (event == ZEBKIT_LOAD_FINISHED)
        zebkit_view_evaluate(view, "document.title", printed, NULL);
}
static void ready(void *data) {
    zebkit_view *view = zebkit_view_new("https://example.com/", 1024, 768);
    zebkit_view_on_load(view, loaded, NULL);
}
int main(int argc, char **argv) {
    return zebkit_main(argc, argv, ready, NULL);
}cc app.c -I$PKG/include -L$PKG -l:libzebkit.so.1 -Wl,-rpath,$PKG -o app   # Linux
cc app.c -I$PKG/include -F$PKG -framework Zebkit -Wl,-rpath,$PKG -o app   # macOS
clang-cl /MT app.c /I%PKG%\include %PKG%\zebkit.dll.lib %PKG%\zebkit_sandbox.lib   # Windows
./app --remote-debugging-port=9222     # with CDP for Puppeteer and Playwright
On Windows the executable takes part in Chromium's sandbox: it links
zebkit_sandbox.lib and calls zebkit_win_startup() first in main()
(docs/WINDOWS.md).
Without unprivileged user namespaces the engine refuses to start and says why: install its
helper, or in a container of its own add --no-sandbox (docs/SANDBOX.md).
The application serves its own pages from a scheme and gives them
functions to call; a page has nothing of zebkit unless it is granted.
/* The page calls zebkit.app.greet("Ada"). */
static void greet(zebkit_view *view, const char *origin, const char *args_json,
                  zebkit_call *call, void *data) {
    char answer[256];
    snprintf(answer, sizeof answer, "{\"hello\": %s}", args_json);
    zebkit_call_resolve(call, answer);
}
/* app://main/... from ./ui, in ranges for media. A real handler refuses "..". */
static void serve(zebkit_request *request, void *data) {
    char path[1024];
    snprintf(path, sizeof path, "ui%s", zebkit_request_url(request) + sizeof "app://main" - 1);
    zebkit_request_respond_file(request, path, NULL);
}
static void closed(zebkit_view *view, void *data) { zebkit_quit(); }
static void ready(void *data) {
    zebkit_view *view = zebkit_view_new("app://main/index.html", 1024, 768);
    zebkit_view_grant(view, "app://main", ZEBKIT_ALLOW_APP | ZEBKIT_ALLOW_PDF, NULL);
    zebkit_view_bind(view, "greet", greet, NULL);
    zebkit_view_on_close(view, closed, NULL);
}
int main(int argc, char **argv) {
    zebkit_scheme_register("app", ZEBKIT_SCHEME_STANDARD | ZEBKIT_SCHEME_SECURE | ZEBKIT_SCHEME_FETCH);
    zebkit_scheme_handle("app", serve, NULL);
    return zebkit_main(argc, argv, ready, NULL);
}
In the page, every call is a promise and bytes are Uint8Arrays:
const reply = await zebkit.app.greet('Ada');            // the application's function
const pdf = await zebkit.pdf.open(await (await fetch('report.pdf')).bytes());
const rgba = await pdf.render(0, {scale: 2});           // a page as pixels
const hits = await pdf.search('revenue');
const packed = await zebkit.compress('zstd', bytes, 19);
const hash = await zebkit.crypto.digest('SHA-256', 'abc');
Each thing the engine would show the person, or ask of the system, has a default that works and a function of the application's that replaces it. Nothing reaches the system without a decision the application can take; without a function, a page gets what a careful browser gives it, and nothing at all where a browser would ask.
import zebkit
zebkit.scheme_register("app")   # served by a scheme_handle(), as in the C example above
zebkit.init(["app"])
# The page is the title bar: the window's buttons over it, dragged by its CSS.
view = zebkit.View("app://main/index.html", 1000, 700, options={
    "frame": "overlay", "controls": {"height": 40, "color": "#1b1d2a", "symbolColor": "#ffffff"},
    "dragRegions": {"source": "css", "origins": ["app://main"]}})
# The application's menu bar (macOS) and keys, with state that changes in place.
zebkit.app_set_menu([{"title": "File", "items": [{"title": "Autosave", "id": "autosave", "checked": True}]}],
                    lambda item: zebkit.app_update_menu_item(item, checked=False))
# A tray icon, the Dock's or the taskbar's badge, and the page's notifications as the application's.
tray = zebkit.Tray(open("icon.png", "rb").read(), "My application")
zebkit.app_set_badge("3")
zebkit.on_notification(lambda event: print("show in my own UI:", event))
# What a page asks for: a USB device, a screen to capture, a colour, a share.
view.on_device_chooser(lambda request: request.respond(request.metadata["devices"][0]["id"]))
view.on_media_access(lambda request: request.respond(True, None, "view"))
view.on_share(lambda request: request.respond(True))
# The system: its theme and its changes, the session's lock, the screens.
zebkit.on_environment_changed(lambda env: print("dark" if env["colorScheme"] == "dark" else "light"))
zebkit.on_power_event(lambda event: print(event["event"]))   # suspend, resume, lock, unlock
print(zebkit.displays())
docs/SYSTEM_INTEGRATION.md has each surface, its default, its status on
each system and why; docs/API.md has the calls in the four languages;
examples/custom-titlebar is a window whose title bar is the page.
zebkit on crates.io, with
zebkit-build to put the engine
beside your program; the build downloads the engine for your system once and
checks its SHA-256.
[dependencies]
zebkit = "0.4.0"
[build-dependencies]
zebkit-build = "0.4.0"// build.rs: puts the engine beside the executable
fn main() { zebkit_build::bundle(); }
// main.rs
fn main() {
    std::process::exit(zebkit::run(|| {
        let view = zebkit::View::new(Some("https://example.com/"), 1024, 768);
        view.grant("https://example.com", zebkit::Allow::APP, None);
        view.bind("greet", |call| {
            let answer = format!("\"hello, {}\"", call.args_json());
            call.resolve(&answer)
        });
        view.on_close(zebkit::quit);
    }));
}
ZEBKIT_DIR points the build at a package (bindings/rust/README.md).

releases of the same version,
with ZEBKIT_DIR pointing at it:
pip install zebkit

zebkit-js runs an ES module on the engine's V8, for applications
written in JavaScript, with views, the same APIs, and native windows:
// zebkit-js main.mjs
const view = new zebkit.View('app://main/index.html', {width: 1024, height: 768});
view.grant('app://main', ['app', 'pdf']);
view.bind('save', async (name, text) => {
  await zebkit.fs.writeFile(`${zebkit.args[0]}/${name}`, text);
  return {saved: true};
});
view.on('close', () => zebkit.quit());// zebkit-js examples/ui/todo.mjs: a window of native widgets, styled with
// Tailwind's classes and kept up to date by signals (an excerpt)
const {h, signal, computed, For, window} = zebkit.ui;
const [tasks, setTasks] = signal([]);
const done = computed(() => tasks().filter((t) => t.done).length);
const Task = (task) =>
  h('view', {class: 'flex-row items-center gap-3 p-3 rounded-xl bg-[#141a2e]'},
    h('button', {class: 'w-8 h-8 p-0 rounded-full bg-[#7c5cff] text-white',
                 onClick: () => toggle(task)}, task.done ? '✓' : ''),
    h('text', {class: 'grow text-[#e6e8f2]'}, task.text));
window({title: 'Today', width: 460, height: 680}, () =>
  h('view', {class: 'flex-col gap-4 p-6 bg-[#0b1020]'},
    h('text', {class: 'text-3xl font-bold text-white'}, 'Ship something great'),
    h('text', {class: 'text-sm text-[#8a91aa]'}, () => `${done()} of ${tasks().length} done`),
    h(For, {each: tasks}, Task)));
Playwright's API runs inside the engine (docs/AUTOMATION.md): every
command of Playwright's protocol, in the application's process, with no
CDP and no Node.js. From C it is one call, zebkit_automation_call(view, "Frame.click", "{\"selector\": \"#go\"}", done, data); Python has it with
Playwright's names:
import zebkit
from zebkit.automation import Page, expect, run
async def test():
    page = Page()
    await page.goto("https://example.com/")
    await expect(page).to_have_title("Example Domain")
    await expect(page.get_by_text("documentation examples")).to_be_visible()
    await page.screenshot(path="example.png")
    zebkit.quit()
zebkit.main(lambda: run(test()), ["python", "--headless"])
Playwright's own clients, its test runner and its other languages included, connect to the engine's Playwright endpoint unchanged:
tools/zebkit-run --headless --playwright-port=0   # prints "Playwright listening on ws://127.0.0.1:<port>/<token>"const browser = await chromium.connect('ws://127.0.0.1:<port>/<token>');
const page = await (await browser.newContext()).newPage();
Agents and tools that speak CDP drive zebkit as they would drive Chrome:
tools/zebkit-run --headless --remote-debugging-port=9222 https://example.com/
Any CDP client connects to http://127.0.0.1:9222.
An MCP client gets the engine's capabilities as tools from tools/zebkit-mcp, a
separate program, with file access and origins denied until its operator grants
them (docs/MCP.md):
ZEBKIT_DIR=<package> cargo build --release --manifest-path tools/zebkit-mcp/Cargo.toml   # or the archive's
zebkit-mcp --allow-origin https://example.com --allow-write ~/agent-files   # on standard input and output
zebkit-mcp --http 8931 --allow-origin '*'                                   # on 127.0.0.1, with a tokenmise example:linux:basic    # examples/window.c: a browser window
mise example:rust:window    # the same in Rust
mise example:ffmpeg         # examples/ffmpeg.cpp: a library inside the engine
(cd examples/gpui-browser && cargo run --release)   # a tabbed browser in GPUI-KIT
Against the latest stable Electron, 45.2.1 (Chromium 156), measured the same way:
one harness, the same pages, two thin hosts that do the same thing, every process
counted, medians of 5 to 11 runs taking turns, Linux x86-64, 2026-11-06 and 07
(scripts/electron-compare.sh, docs/reports/electron-compare.md).
- Size. zebkit keeps the whole web platform applications use: HTML, CSS, JavaScript with every JIT tier, WebAssembly, WebGL, media with H.264 and AAC, HTTP/3, PDF.
- Speed. Chrome's own profile-guided optimization reaches Blink because
zebkit is built with CFI as Chrome is; every speed change is kept only when it
gains more than it costs in size (docs/SIZE_AND_SPEED.md).
- Where Electron is ahead: one process fewer a page, and memory on two of the ten sites, YouTube and The Verge, where advertising and video decide.
- How each number is made: docs/SIZE_AND_SPEED.md.
The same Playwright commands three ways, headless, medians
(docs/reports/automation-bench.md, scripts/automation-bench.sh):
- zebkit's API, in-process: your program calls the command through
<zebkit/automation.h>, Python's zebkit.automation or Rust's zebkit::automation; it runs inside the engine, with no Node.js and no protocol.
- Your Playwright scripts, connected to zebkit: Playwright's own Node.js
client, unchanged, with chromium.connect() to zebkit's endpoint; its test
suite (v1.64.1) passes 4,046 of its tests there, Chrome 4,196
(docs/AUTOMATION.md, section 7).
- Playwright with Chrome: Playwright as usual, over CDP.
- Why it is faster: one call in the renderer where Playwright's server makes several round trips over CDP, no JSON between processes, no Node.js process (Playwright's alone reached 175 MiB); and the frames a click's checks wait for are made at once instead of at 60 Hz on a page without a display.
- A screenshot is 2.7 times faster: the fresh frame it takes is made at
once instead of at the next 60 Hz tick, the PNG is deflated at level 1 with
the Up filter (2 ms where Chrome's default level takes 13, for 59 KB
instead of 40 KB on this page), and the picture's shared memory is made in
one call instead of a page fault at a time. What is left of the 12 ms is the
page's frame (4 ms), copying the picture out of the compositor (4 ms) and
encoding it (4 ms). The pixels themselves, with no encoding
(zebkit_automation_screenshot_pixels(), zebkit's own), take 9 ms. Over CDP
zebkit does what Chrome does: frames at 60 Hz, Chrome's PNG.
upstream/ (Chromium's tree, about 30 GB), out/, dist/ and .cache/
are generated and not tracked.
zebkit is Chromium plus a small patch set (patches/), built from source.
Where Chromium lacks something an application needs, zebkit patches
Chromium rather than working around it (docs/BUILD.md).
zebkit is free software under the GNU Lesser General Public License, version 2.1 or (at your option) any later version: LICENSE. Applications of any license, open or closed, can use it as a library.
The engine contains Chromium and the libraries it uses (Blink, V8, Skia,
PDFium, FFmpeg in its LGPL configuration, ICU, SQLite, BoringSSL and others),
each under its own license. Every release archive carries LICENSE, a
NOTICE that says where its source is, and THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.txt with
every third-party license text. docs/LICENSING.md says
what an application that ships zebkit has to do.
Contributions are accepted under the same license: by sending a pull request you agree that your contribution is licensed under the LGPL 2.1 or later, as the rest of zebkit.
